ocar.opportunity: Connectomics and neuronal diversity studies now produce enough morphology data that a computational taxonomy of neuron shapes is within reach. A shared map of which methods work, on what representations, and how they are scored would help the field compare results instead of inventing new classifiers in isolation.
ocar.challenge: Neuron taxonomy is still hard because morphology is high-dimensional and published classifiers differ in features, representations, and evaluation. Without a structured synthesis it is unclear which computational approaches actually dominate and whether reported accuracy is comparable across studies.
ocar.action: In Neuroscience in 2026, Lobato, Leite, Jacob, and Santana ran a systematic review of peer-reviewed neuronal morphology classification papers published since 2018. They screened 840 papers from five databases (2018–2024), applied predefined quality criteria on study design, methodology, and reporting, and extracted methods, representations, and evaluation metrics from the 35 studies that met those standards.
ocar.resolution: Artificial neural networks were the main classification method (21 papers). Microscopy-image representations used to extract morphometric features were common (30 papers), and accuracy was the predominant evaluation measure (29 papers). The review therefore supplies an up-to-date snapshot of how in silico morphology classifiers are built and scored.
ocar.future_work: The authors frame the review as a guide for future neuroscience classification work. A natural next step is to move beyond accuracy-dominated reporting toward shared representations and evaluation protocols that make new methods comparable.

summaries.beginner: Scientists want computers to sort brain cells by their branching shapes, but labs have used many different recipes. This review gathered recent papers and reports which computer methods, image types, and scores are used most often.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroscience in 2026, Lobato and colleagues systematically reviewed in silico neuronal morphology classification. From 840 papers published between 2018 and 2024 they retained 35 studies that met predefined quality criteria. Artificial neural networks were the leading method (21 papers), morphometric features from microscopy images were the usual representation (30 papers), and accuracy was the usual metric (29 papers). The paper is a methods map rather than a new classifier.
summaries.advanced: Inclusion was restricted to peer-reviewed work since 2018 that passed a risk-of-bias screen, so earlier classical morphometrics and many conference papers are out of scope. Dominance of accuracy does not imply that accuracy is the right metric for imbalanced cell-type taxonomies. The review reports counts of methods and representations, not a head-to-head benchmark on a shared dataset.

plain_language_summary: Scientists want computers to sort brain cells by their branching shapes, but labs have used many different recipes. This review gathered recent papers and reports which computer methods, image types, and scores are used most often.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain calcium imaging in C. elegans records population activity under changing stimuli, offering a chance to recover directed, lag-specific circuit interactions without assuming a parametric dynamical model.
ocar.challenge: Local, short-latency interactions unfold across multiple timescales and contexts. Pairwise analyses omit intermediate lags, and parametric models of the underlying dynamics can be misspecified.
ocar.action: Kinger, Bertram, Dyballa, Yemini, and Zucker introduce Score-Block Time Graphs (SBTG). Denoising score models estimate joint-window scores over consecutive activity snapshots; cross-block score products become calibrated directed-edge tests that recover the Jacobian of the transition map. Minimal multi-block windows condition on intermediate time points to separate lag-specific effects.
ocar.resolution: Applied to whole-brain C. elegans calcium imaging, SBTG recovered lag-specific circuit structure not resolved by current methods, including improved alignment with independent connectomes, cell-type-specific temporal organization, and neuromodulatory profiles consistent with known receptor kinetics.
ocar.future_work: The authors position SBTG as a practical tool for turning high-dimensional recordings into statistically testable circuit hypotheses. Broader use on other stimuli and datasets would test how far the recovered edges generalize.

summaries.beginner: This paper offers a way to guess which worm brain cells talk to which others, and with what delay, from movies of their activity. The method does not need a fixed equation for how the brain changes from moment to moment.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 paper, Kinger and colleagues present SBTG, which uses denoising score models on consecutive C. elegans activity windows and converts score products into directed, lag-specific edge tests. Multi-block windows are meant to avoid omitted-lag bias in pairwise analyses. On whole-brain calcium imaging the method improved alignment with independent worm connectomes and recovered cell-type and neuromodulatory temporal structure.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not report quantitative alignment scores or a named comparison method, so the claimed improvement over current methods should be read as qualitative. SBTG infers statistical directed interactions from sampled activity, not necessarily anatomical synapses. Results are tied to C. elegans calcium imaging under varying stimuli.

plain_language_summary: This paper offers a way to guess which worm brain cells talk to which others, and with what delay, from movies of their activity. The method does not need a fixed equation for how the brain changes from moment to moment.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome-constrained network models can match behavior without matching biology, so the field needs a population-level fidelity metric that asks whether internal representations, not just outputs, reflect real wiring.
ocar.challenge: Behavioral tests cannot tell real wiring from arbitrary wiring. Brunton and colleagues (2026) showed a C. elegans connectome trained with deep reinforcement learning can produce realistic fly walking, which makes a decoder-free metric urgent.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2026, Zhou and Hasler apply representational similarity analysis and centered kernel alignment to the Flyvis pretrained Drosophila visual-system ensemble (50 connectome-constrained networks versus 50 stability-constrained random baselines). They also attempt untrained-network and trained-random-wiring tests against a T4/T5 direction-tuning reference.
ocar.resolution: Connectome-constrained networks produced smoother circular direction geometry than random networks (RSA Spearman r = 0.686 for ON edges and r = 0.846 for ON+OFF edges). The authors withdraw earlier untrained-network correlations as permutation tests on rounding. The decisive test—discriminating real wiring from trained random wiring—was attempted but remains unresolved because the available biological reference is dominated by circular stimulus structure.
ocar.future_work: They offer representational geometry as a candidate fidelity metric and sketch a path toward metrics that could scale to mammalian-cortex-sized emulations, pending a biological reference that can support the trained-random comparison.

summaries.beginner: A model can walk like a fly even if its inner wiring is wrong. These authors test whether the pattern of how groups of model cells respond to moving edges can tell real fly wiring from shuffled wiring.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv preprint, Zhou and Hasler propose representational geometry as a fidelity metric for connectome-constrained networks, motivated by Brunton et al. (2026). Using Flyvis Drosophila visual-system models, connectome-constrained networks showed stronger circular direction geometry than random baselines (RSA r = 0.686 ON; r = 0.846 ON+OFF). Comparisons to a Maisak et al. 2013 T4/T5 reference and to trained random wiring collapsed to circularity confounds, so the decisive test remains open.
summaries.advanced: The catalog tags list C. elegans, but the experiments are on Flyvis Drosophila visual networks reconstructed from partial electron-microscopy sources. Untrained connectome-constrained RDMs had dynamic range below float32 round-off; earlier p-values on those matrices are withdrawn. Partialling circular structure left residuals that were not significant at n = 50. Experiment 5 (degree-preserving versus degree-breaking trained nulls, n = 10 each) inherited the same circularity confound. Numbers should be cited only as reported for this ensemble and stimulus set.

plain_language_summary: A model can walk like a fly even if its inner wiring is wrong. These authors test whether the pattern of how groups of model cells respond to moving edges can tell real fly wiring from shuffled wiring.

ocar.opportunity: Electron-microscopy connectomes now span multiple species, so machine learning could in principle read evolutionary design signatures from simple single-neuron measurements rather than from full deep networks.
ocar.challenge: Cross-species datasets are heterogeneous, missing values invite imputation artifacts, and it is unclear whether minimal features such as cable length and synapse count carry phylogenetic signal or reconstruction error.
ocar.action: At the 2026 International Conference on Bioinformatics & Computational Biology, Kawada unified eight electron-microscopy reconstructions spanning five species (N = 176,914 neurons) across about 500 million years of evolution. A random forest was trained on low-dimensional features (cable length, synapse count, synaptic partner count) and interpreted with SHAP; imputation effects and unsupervised clustering were also tested.
ocar.resolution: The classifier reached 92.2% accuracy versus a 60.7% linear baseline (McNemar’s χ² = 9153.78, p < 10⁻⁴), with SHAP showing species-specific feature effects such as neurite length hurting zebrafish labels but helping mouse labels. Imputing missing local density inflated feature importance by 76.9%. In C. elegans, unsupervised clustering revealed hidden subpopulations with conflicting wiring rules.
ocar.future_work: The paper offers a validated, artifact-aware framework for comparative connectomics. Next uses should keep missing-value handling explicit and test whether the same minimal features remain phylogenetically informative on new reconstructions.

summaries.beginner: Researchers asked whether a few simple measurements of each nerve cell, such as how long it is and how many contacts it makes, can tell which animal it came from. A standard machine-learning model did well, but filling in missing numbers could trick the model.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 IEEE bioinformatics conference paper, Kawada analyzed eight EM connectomes from five species (176,914 neurons). A random forest on cable length, synapse count, and partner count reached 92.2% species accuracy versus 60.7% for a linear baseline. SHAP highlighted species-specific feature effects, while imputing missing local density raised feature importance by 76.9%. C. elegans clustering exposed conflicting wiring-rule subpopulations.
summaries.advanced: Accuracy is for species classification from minimal features, not for cell-type identity. The linear baseline gap is large, but McNemar’s test on such N will almost always be significant; the practical claim is the SHAP species effects and the imputation artifact. Dataset tags include C. elegans and zebrafish; the abstract also discusses mouse. Reconstruction artifacts remain a plausible alternative source of ‘phylogenetic’ signal.

plain_language_summary: Researchers asked whether a few simple measurements of each nerve cell, such as how long it is and how many contacts it makes, can tell which animal it came from. A standard machine-learning model did well, but filling in missing numbers could trick the model.

ocar.opportunity: The H01 electron-microscopy connectome of human temporal cortex makes it possible to ask whether the spatial layout of synapses, not only their weights, helps keep learning stable.
ocar.challenge: How spatial organization of synapses contributes to stable learning has remained a basic open question, and it was unclear whether a structural motif from human cortex could transfer into artificial networks.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2026, Zhu, Chen, Zhao, Xiong, Peng, Wu, and Zhang measured dendritic-spine clustering and synaptic-weight geometry in H01, formalized the pattern as a regularized Hebbian model, and translated it into Spatial Synaptic Regularization (SSR) for artificial networks.
ocar.resolution: Spines clustered morphologically, while synaptic weights showed a center-elevated, surround-suppressed arrangement along dendrites. In the model, strong synapses lowered the chance that neighbors reached high-weight states. SSR reduced forgetting and stabilized learning on continual visual learning, large language-model knowledge editing, and parameter-efficient vision-language adaptation by preserving high-rank, low-overlap representations.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue that spatial synaptic organization is an unrecognized dimension for stabilizing learning. Testing SSR on additional tasks and asking how tightly the H01 motif must be matched would show how general the principle is.

summaries.beginner: Looking at a map of connections in human brain tissue, the authors noticed that strong contacts tend to sit in a bump-and-surround pattern along a branch. Copying that pattern as a rule helped artificial networks forget less while learning new things.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv preprint, Zhu and colleagues used the H01 EM connectome of human temporal cortex to show morphological spine clustering and a center-surround synaptic-weight motif. A regularized Hebbian model captured the idea that strong synapses suppress neighbors. As Spatial Synaptic Regularization, the rule stabilized continual visual learning, LLM knowledge editing, and vision-language adaptation.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not report numerical forgetting reductions, so those gains should not be quantified from this card. H01 is human temporal cortex; transfer to other areas is untested here. SSR’s benefit is attributed to high-rank, low-overlap representations, which is a modeling interpretation of the connectomic motif rather than a causal in vivo test.

plain_language_summary: Looking at a map of connections in human brain tissue, the authors noticed that strong contacts tend to sit in a bump-and-surround pattern along a branch. Copying that pattern as a rule helped artificial networks forget less while learning new things.

ocar.opportunity: The cerebellum is now implicated in cognition and affect as well as motor control, so a comprehensive, directed map of its connections would give systems neuroscience a missing counterpart to cerebral connectomes.
ocar.challenge: Cerebellar connectivity remains undercharacterized relative to cortex, and building a weighted, hierarchical subnetwork from scattered tract-tracing reports is a large collation and graph-filtering problem.
ocar.action: In Cerebellum in 2026, Schmitt, Morawska, Prathapan, and Eipert built a cerebellar connectome from a meta-analytic database of over 7,800 high-resolution tract-tracing studies in rat, using the neuroVIISAS framework. The pipeline included region expansion, graph-theoretical filtering, and edge weighting by anatomical significance, plus lateralization and interhemispheric projections.
ocar.resolution: The network comprises 862 regions and over 21,000 edges, with small-world and scale-free mesoscale properties and non-random microcircuits from motif and modularity analyses. Local metrics highlighted integrative hubs in brainstem-cerebellar loops. Vulnerability analysis showed that removing high-significance edges rapidly degraded clustering, unlike rewired surrogates, pointing to structurally privileged bottlenecks.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the map as a foundation for multimodal, dynamic, and cross-species work. They state that integrating neuronal dynamics, synaptic plasticity, and gene expression will be essential for translational use in health and disease.

summaries.beginner: This paper builds a large wiring diagram of the rat cerebellum from thousands of older tracing studies. It finds both tightly knit local groups and a few bottleneck links that, if cut, quickly scramble the network.
summaries.intermediate: In Cerebellum in 2026, Schmitt, Morawska, Prathapan, and Eipert assembled a directed, weighted rat cerebellar connectome from more than 7,800 tract-tracing studies via neuroVIISAS. The graph has 862 regions and over 21,000 edges, including lateralization and interhemispheric projections after region expansion and anatomical edge weighting. Analyses reported small-world and scale-free structure, integrative brainstem-cerebellar hubs, and faster loss of clustering when high-significance edges were removed than in rewired surrogates.
summaries.advanced: This is a meta-analytic tract-tracing connectome in rat, not an electron-microscopy synapse map; ‘other’ in the organism tag reflects that. Small-world and scale-free labels depend on the filtering and weighting pipeline. Vulnerability is defined against rewired surrogates, so it is a statement about this weighted graph, not about live cerebellar computation.

plain_language_summary: This paper builds a large wiring diagram of the rat cerebellum from thousands of older tracing studies. It finds both tightly knit local groups and a few bottleneck links that, if cut, quickly scramble the network.

ocar.opportunity: Human cortical neurons have more elaborate neurite shapes than rodent neurons, even beyond what size alone explains, offering a morphological handle on why human local connectomes look more complex.
ocar.challenge: Electrophysiology and anatomy differ between human and rodent circuits, but it has been unclear how neurite geometry maps onto synaptic connectivity in the local microcircuit, because potential contacts are not the same as actual synapses.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2026, Barros-Zulaica and colleagues predicted local connectomes from reconstructed human and rodent morphologies, treating axonal and dendritic geometry as a constraint on potential synaptic locations, then compared predicted complexity with experimentally measured connectomes and examined synapse-formation rules including a Hebbian-compatible process.
ocar.resolution: Connectomes predicted from human morphologies had higher complexity on several functionally relevant measures. Morphology-derived potential connectivity could generate non-random clustered structure seen in experimental connectomes, and human neuron shapes strengthened that process. A synapse-formation process compatible with Hebbian plasticity produced the highest complexity and the best match to experimental patterns.
ocar.future_work: Because potential connectivity is only a constraint on actual synapses, a next step is to test which formation rules best match additional human microcircuit measurements.

summaries.beginner: Human brain cells have bushier branches than rodent cells. This study asks whether those shapes alone make the local wiring more clustered and complex, and finds that they can.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv preprint, Barros-Zulaica, Egas Santander, Kanari, and colleagues compared predicted local connectomes from human versus rodent reconstructed morphologies. Human shapes yielded higher complexity on measures previously linked to function, and helped explain clustered, non-random structure in experimental connectomes. Among formation rules considered, a Hebbian-compatible process matched experimental patterns best.
summaries.advanced: Potential connectivity is explicitly not actual synaptic connectivity; the paper treats it as informative but incomplete. Complexity measures are described as functionally relevant from prior work, not re-validated here. No numerical complexity scores appear in the abstract. Organism tags are empty; the comparison is human versus rodent cortical morphologies.

plain_language_summary: Human brain cells have bushier branches than rodent cells. This study asks whether those shapes alone make the local wiring more clustered and complex, and finds that they can.

ocar.opportunity: Large, well-documented visual connectomes now exist for mouse visual cortex and the fruit-fly optic lobe, so synaptic-weight histograms can be compared across distant species as a clue to learning rules.
ocar.challenge: Weight distributions are variously reported as power-law or lognormal, and the degree of proofreading can change how heavy the tails look, which muddies biological interpretation.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (posted 2025; dated 2026 in this catalog), Cirunay, Papp, and Ódor analyzed global synaptic weights and local node strengths in those two visual connectomes, related tail heaviness to proofreading, and invoked a generalized central-limit argument for the lognormal-versus-power-law debate.
ocar.resolution: Global weight distributions showed power-law tails with exponents α ≥ 3 (heavy-tailed but regular), while weights around broadcaster and integrator neurons could be fit with α < 3 (scale-free fat tails). Node-strength distributions showed dual power-law scaling tied mainly to degree heterogeneity; edge-weight assignment was non-random but correlated below 1% with that pattern. Proofreading strongly affected tail heaviness.
ocar.future_work: Because proofreading changes tails, later comparisons should report reconstruction completeness alongside exponents. The dual scaling and hub-associated fat tails are offered as hints about critical learning mechanisms rather than as a finished learning-rule identification.

summaries.beginner: The authors look at how strong the contacts are in a mouse visual-cortex map and a fruit-fly optic-lobe map. Most contacts follow one statistical pattern, but a few hub cells have extra-heavy tails, and how thoroughly the map was cleaned changes the picture.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 bioRxiv paper, Cirunay, Papp, and Ódor compared synaptic-weight statistics in mouse visual cortex and the male fruit-fly optic lobe. Global weights followed power-law tails with α ≥ 3, while source and sink neighborhoods could show α < 3. Proofreading changed tail heaviness, and node strengths showed dual scaling driven mainly by degree heterogeneity, with edge weights modulating the pattern despite correlation below 1%.
summaries.advanced: α values and the <1% correlation are as stated in the abstract; no other numerical exponents are given here. Power-law versus lognormal remains a fitting debate; the authors offer a generalized-CLT explanation rather than a decisive model-selection table. Organism tag lists mouse; the study is explicitly comparative with fly. Results are specific to these two visual volumes.

plain_language_summary: The authors look at how strong the contacts are in a mouse visual-cortex map and a fruit-fly optic-lobe map. Most contacts follow one statistical pattern, but a few hub cells have extra-heavy tails, and how thoroughly the map was cleaned changes the picture.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes across species now share statistical regularities—exponential wiring lengths, heavy-tailed lognormal node strengths, and power-law functional tails—that look like signatures of a brain near criticality.
ocar.challenge: Those features emerge from bottom-up organization, so it is unclear whether a single self-organizing model can produce both power-law edge weights and lognormal node strengths without precise external tuning.
ocar.action: In Scientific Reports in 2025, Cirunay, Batac, and Ódor ran a sandpile-like avalanche model on hierarchical modular networks that mimic neuronal circuitry, then added Hebbian learning in which neurons that fire together wire together.
ocar.resolution: Avalanches produced robust power-law size distributions with critical exponent 3/2, characteristic of neuronal systems. With Hebbian learning, the model recovered power-law edge-weight distributions and lognormal node-degree distributions comparable to connectome data.
ocar.future_work: The results are offered as support for a critical brain whose local interactions drive connectivity and learning. Testing the same growth rule on additional empirical connectome statistics would show how much of the phenomenology is captured.

summaries.beginner: Real brain wiring maps share odd statistical patterns, as if the network were poised at a tipping point. A simple model in which activity avalanches and cells that fire together strengthen their links reproduced those patterns.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports in 2025, Cirunay, Batac, and Ódor combined a sandpile-like model on hierarchical modular networks with Hebbian learning. Avalanche sizes followed a power law with exponent 3/2, and learning recovered power-law edge weights and lognormal node degrees comparable to published connectome statistics. The authors interpret this as self-organized criticality without external fine-tuning.
summaries.advanced: The exponent 3/2 is reported as characteristic of neuronal avalanches from prior literature as well as this model. ‘Comparable to connectome data’ is qualitative in the abstract; no goodness-of-fit numbers are given. Hierarchical modular networks are simulated stand-ins for circuitry, not reconstructed EM graphs. Criticality here is a statistical-physics analogy, not a direct physiological measurement.

plain_language_summary: Real brain wiring maps share odd statistical patterns, as if the network were poised at a tipping point. A simple model in which activity avalanches and cells that fire together strengthen their links reproduced those patterns.

ocar.opportunity: The recently released full Drosophila connectome supplies both topology and synaptic weights that could be used as a reservoir for time-series prediction instead of a randomly wired echo-state network.
ocar.challenge: The full connectome is large, so a computationally convenient reservoir must select neurons—either preserving or breaking documented class proportions—while still testing whether biology-derived wiring helps.
ocar.action: In Biomimetics in 2025, Costi, Hadjiivanov, Dold, Hale, and Izzo built echo-state connectivity from the fly connectome, kept the most connected neurons under two selection criteria, and compared performance with state-of-the-art reservoirs, hybrid topology/weight controls, and a run that used the entire connectome.
ocar.resolution: Connectome-based reservoirs were significantly more resilient to overfitting than standard implementations, especially in already overfitting-prone cases. Both topology and weights contributed. Using the entire connectome, despite many more trained parameters, stayed resilient and reached a normalized error under 2% at lower regularization than other reservoirs trained with higher regularization.
ocar.future_work: The hybrid ablations isolate topology versus weights but leave open how far the overfitting resilience transfers to other tasks beyond multivariate chaotic time-series prediction.

summaries.beginner: The authors used the fruit fly’s real wiring diagram as the hidden web inside a forecasting computer model. That biologically inspired web was less prone to memorizing noise than a typical random web, even when it had more tunable knobs.
summaries.intermediate: In Biomimetics in 2025, Costi and colleagues turned the Drosophila connectome into an echo-state reservoir for multivariate chaotic time-series prediction, selecting the most connected neurons with or without preserving neuron-class proportions. Connectome reservoirs overfit less than standard ones; hybrids showed that both topology and weights matter. The full-connectome reservoir kept normalized error under 2% at lower regularization than more heavily regularized baselines.
summaries.advanced: The <2% normalized error applies to the full-connectome experiment at lower regularization, not to every subsampled reservoir. ‘Significantly more resilient’ is not given a p-value in the abstract. Task domain is chaotic time-series prediction, not fly behavior. Selection of ‘most connected neurons’ is a degree filter that may itself drive robustness.

plain_language_summary: The authors used the fruit fly’s real wiring diagram as the hidden web inside a forecasting computer model. That biologically inspired web was less prone to memorizing noise than a typical random web, even when it had more tunable knobs.

ocar.opportunity: Simulations of morphologically detailed networks let researchers manipulate synaptic connectivity in ways experiments cannot, so causal tests of non-random connectome features become possible.
ocar.challenge: Non-random synaptic trends sit at a fine scale that is hard to perturb in tissue. Replacing or transplanting connectomes in large models needs a reproducible, parameterized workflow.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2024, Pokorny, Awile, Isbister, Kurban, Wolf, and Reimann introduce Connectome-Manipulator, a Python framework for creating, fitting, and swapping SONATA-format connectomes, including stochastic models fit to existing connectivity. They used it in a detailed rat somatosensory-cortex model to transplant interneuron trends from electron microscopy and to simplify excitatory connectomes.
ocar.resolution: Network simulations of those two use cases produced diverse shifts in the activity of individual neuron populations that were causally linked to the manipulations.
ocar.future_work: The framework is meant for systematic structure–function studies. Applying the same transplants and simplifications to other SONATA models would test how specific the reported activity shifts are to this rat somatosensory circuit.

summaries.beginner: This software lets scientists rewrite the wiring in a large computer model of cortex and then watch what the cells do. Changing inhibitory and excitatory connection patterns shifted which cell groups were active.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, Pokorny, Awile, Isbister, Kurban, Wolf, and Reimann describe Connectome-Manipulator, a Python tool for SONATA network models. It can fit stochastic connectivity, replace a connectome with simpler equivalents, or transplant features between connectomes. In a detailed rat somatosensory cortex model, transplanting electron-microscopy interneuron trends and simplifying excitatory connectivity produced population-specific activity shifts attributed to those edits.
summaries.advanced: Causal claims are simulation-internal: activity changes follow the intended rewiring in this model, not in vivo perturbations. The abstract does not quantify the activity shifts. Organism tag is ‘other’; the worked example is rat somatosensory cortex. Electron microscopy appears as the source of transplanted interneuron trends, not as a new reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: This software lets scientists rewrite the wiring in a large computer model of cortex and then watch what the cells do. Changing inhibitory and excitatory connection patterns shifted which cell groups were active.

ocar.opportunity: A whole-brain fly connectome plus calcium imaging can be combined at the first hops of taste processing, where unifying coding principles have been hard to see because taste influences many behaviors through distributed circuits.
ocar.challenge: Taste responses are spread across fly brain circuits that drive feeding, oviposition, locomotion, mating, and memory, which has hindered attempts to deduce shared organizing rules.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2024, Li, Dhaliwal, Stanley, Junca, and Gordon aligned whole-brain connectivity with functional calcium imaging of early taste circuits, examining cholinergic and GABAergic local interneurons postsynaptic to labellar sensory neurons and the taste projection neurons they feed.
ocar.resolution: Taste-quality representation stayed largely segregated in those local interneurons. Some taste projection neurons received direct sensory input, but many received primarily indirect input via cholinergic local neurons, which appeared to act as nodes feeding dedicated sets of morphologically similar projection neurons. A small set of representative projection neurons still showed mostly segregated taste information.
ocar.future_work: The authors describe a previously unappreciated logic in fly taste circuits. Broader sampling of projection-neuron types would test how far segregation holds beyond the representative cells examined.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies taste with cells on their mouthparts, and those signals fan out through the brain. This study finds that different tastes stay surprisingly separate in the first brain cells that receive them, rather than being immediately mixed.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, Li and colleagues combined the Drosophila whole-brain connectome with calcium imaging of early taste circuits. Taste quality remained largely segregated in cholinergic and GABAergic local interneurons postsynaptic to labellar sensory neurons. Cholinergic local neurons often provided the main feedforward path onto morphologically similar taste projection neurons, which also kept tastes mostly separate in the sampled set.
summaries.advanced: Segregation is reported as ‘largely’ and ‘mostly’ from a small number of representative projection neurons, not a complete census. Functional imaging and connectivity are combined but the abstract does not specify the imaging sample size. Organism is fly; no registry dataset is tagged.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies taste with cells on their mouthparts, and those signals fan out through the brain. This study finds that different tastes stay surprisingly separate in the first brain cells that receive them, rather than being immediately mixed.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans is small enough that structure and physiology can be studied together, but only if activity traces and wiring diagrams from different labs are put into a common format.
ocar.challenge: Physiology datasets use distinct formats and protocols, and connectome annotations need preprocessing before analysis, blocking cross-lab modeling.
ocar.action: In a 2024 paper, Simeon, Kashyap, Kording, and Boyden compiled neural activity from 12 neuroimaging experiments and connectivity from 9 connectome annotations based on 3 primary electron-microscopy studies and 1 signal-propagation study. A pipeline standardized neuron order and resampled traces to a common rate. The collection is released on HuggingFace.
ocar.resolution: The homogenized physiology set covers recordings from approximately 900 worms and 250 uniquely labeled neurons. Connectomes are represented as graphs of the entire nervous system. The resource is intended for modern neural-network analyses of structure–function relationships and for cross-lab, cross-animal comparison.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the compilation as a starting point for modeling; downstream users still need to respect protocol differences that remain after resampling.

summaries.beginner: Many labs have filmed worm neurons or mapped their wiring, but the files did not match. This team cleaned and aligned those datasets so they can be compared and used to train models.
summaries.intermediate: In 2024, Simeon, Kashyap, Kording, and Boyden released homogenized C. elegans activity and connectivity data. Twelve neuroimaging experiments were standardized (neuron order and sampling rate), yielding recordings from about 900 worms and 250 uniquely labeled neurons. Connectivity comes from nine annotations of three primary EM studies plus one signal-propagation study, posted on HuggingFace for structure–function modeling.
summaries.advanced: ‘Approximately 900 worms and 250 uniquely labeled neurons’ are the homogenized physiology counts; not every worm has all 250 cells labeled. Connectome graphs mix EM reconstructions and a signal-propagation study, which are not the same measurement. No journal is listed in this catalog row. Resampling does not remove protocol differences in stimuli or labeling.

plain_language_summary: Many labs have filmed worm neurons or mapped their wiring, but the files did not match. This team cleaned and aligned those datasets so they can be compared and used to train models.

ocar.opportunity: Aggression includes both shared and sex-specific actions, so identifying neurons that drive the shared component in both male and female flies would split monomorphic from dimorphic circuitry.
ocar.challenge: How the brain implements sexually monomorphic versus dimorphic aggressive actions is poorly understood, and most known fly aggression neurons express fruitless, a sex-differentiation gene.
ocar.action: In Journal of Neuroscience in 2024, Tao, Ayambem, Barranca, and Bhandawat tested CL062 neurons, previously linked to male aggression, in females, and examined fruitless expression plus connectivity in a female electron-microscopy dataset.
ocar.resolution: CL062 neurons also mediate female aggression, acting acutely and without a target present; the same action set is elicited in both sexes, though overall behavior remains sexually dimorphic. CL062 neurons do not express fruitless. Connectomics in the female EM volume suggested limited connections to known fruitless aggression neurons and different descending targets, placing CL062 in a parallel monomorphic circuit.
ocar.future_work: The parallel-circuit claim is based on one female EM dataset and limited connections; mapping the corresponding male wiring and downstream motor paths would test how fully the pathway is shared.

summaries.beginner: Some fly brain cells that make males fight also make females fight, and they work even when no other fly is nearby. Those cells seem to sit on a shared pathway, separate from the better-known sex-specific fighting circuit.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience in 2024, Tao and colleagues show that CL062 neurons, already known to drive male Drosophila aggression, also drive female aggression acutely and without a target. The elicited actions are shared but overall behavior remains sexually dimorphic. CL062 lacks fruitless, and female EM connectomics indicated limited coupling to known fruitless aggression neurons and distinct descending partners.
summaries.advanced: Connectomic conclusions are from a female EM dataset and are described as ‘limited connections’ and ‘suggests,’ not a full circuit proof. No synapse counts appear in the abstract. Parallelism with dimorphic circuits is an interpretation of that wiring plus the fruitless-negative molecular identity.

plain_language_summary: Some fly brain cells that make males fight also make females fight, and they work even when no other fly is nearby. Those cells seem to sit on a shared pathway, separate from the better-known sex-specific fighting circuit.

ocar.opportunity: A cubic millimeter of mouse cortex reconstructed by electron microscopy contains tens of thousands of neurons, including many incomplete cells, so a soma-centered classifier could still assign types across an entire volume.
ocar.challenge: Most neurons in large EM volumes have incomplete reconstructions, which blocks type assignment methods that need full arbors, even though EM offers unbiased ultrastructure and connectivity.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2024 catalog year), Elabbady and colleagues systematically surveyed the somatic region of all cells in a cubic millimeter of cortex (MICrONS) using quantitative EM features, then used those labels to characterize cell-type-specific connectivity and to find rare wiring patterns.
ocar.resolution: Perisomatic features were surprisingly sufficient to identify cell types, including types defined mainly by connectivity. The classification enabled cell-type-specific connectivity characterization and localization of cells with rare connectivity patterns in the dataset.
ocar.future_work: The survey is a practical route through incomplete reconstructions; applying the same perisomatic features to other large EM volumes would test how far the sufficiency claim travels.

summaries.beginner: In a huge electron-microscope map of mouse cortex, many cells are only partly traced. The authors show that looking just around the cell body is often enough to tell what kind of cell it is, including types defined by how they connect.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, Elabbady and MICrONS colleagues quantified perisomatic electron-microscopy features for all cells in a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex. Those features classified cell types, including types defined mainly by connectivity, despite incomplete arbors. The labels then supported type-specific connectivity analysis and searches for rare wiring patterns in the volume.
summaries.advanced: ‘Surprising sufficiency’ is qualitative; the abstract does not report classification accuracy. Types include those ‘defined primarily based on their connectivity patterns,’ so some labels are partly circular with the connectivity they later characterize. Results are for this MICrONS cubic-millimeter volume.

plain_language_summary: In a huge electron-microscope map of mouse cortex, many cells are only partly traced. The authors show that looking just around the cell body is often enough to tell what kind of cell it is, including types defined by how they connect.

ocar.opportunity: The MICrONS millimeter-scale cortical reconstruction lets excitation and inhibition be examined inside large neuron motifs, not only as pairwise averages.
ocar.challenge: Assemblies are often imagined as internally excitatory, with inhibition treated as untargeted blanket suppression. Pairwise connectivity may miss higher-order targeting.
ocar.action: In Cerebral Cortex in 2024 (catalog journal field lists bioRxiv), Reimann, Egas Santander, Ecker, and Muller analyzed excitatory and inhibitory structure in the MICrONS mm³ electron-microscopy dataset, focusing on large non-random motifs and where inhibitory neurons attach along those sequences.
ocar.resolution: Excitation was organized around feed-forward flow in large motifs, from few sources to more potential targets. Inhibitory neurons connected at specific sequential positions, implementing targeted, symmetrical competition. None of these trends were detectable in pairwise connectivity alone.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue this higher-order inhibitory targeting has implications for learning and synaptic plasticity. Direct physiological tests of the predicted competition are the obvious next measurement.

summaries.beginner: In a detailed map of a speck of mouse cortex, excitatory cells form one-way chains, and inhibitory cells plug into particular steps of those chains. That targeted braking does not show up if you only look at pairs of cells.
summaries.intermediate: In 2024, Reimann and colleagues analyzed the MICrONS mm³ cortical connectome and found large non-random excitatory motifs with feed-forward flow from few sources to more targets. Inhibitory neurons attached at specific motif positions, creating targeted symmetrical competition invisible in pairwise statistics. They interpret this as higher-order inhibitory specificity rather than blanket inhibition.
summaries.advanced: The venue in this catalog row is listed as bioRxiv while the DOI is Cerebral Cortex; cite as the 2024 connectome analysis of MICrONS mm³. ‘Symmetrical competition’ is a wiring interpretation, not a measured activity effect. Trends are undetectable pairwise by the authors’ analysis; that depends on their motif definition. Implications for plasticity are stated, not tested.

plain_language_summary: In a detailed map of a speck of mouse cortex, excitatory cells form one-way chains, and inhibitory cells plug into particular steps of those chains. That targeted braking does not show up if you only look at pairs of cells.

ocar.opportunity: Counting and mapping Gray type I/II, or asymmetric versus symmetric, synapses in cortex is central to excitatory/inhibitory organization, and volume electron microscopy can in principle classify every synapse in a 3D block.
ocar.challenge: Potassium ferrocyanide, used to darken membranes in volume EM, thins postsynaptic densities as concentration rises, making symmetric synapses especially hard to identify unambiguously.
ocar.action: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy in 2024, Cano-Astorga, Plaza-Alonso, Turégano-Lopez, Rodrigo-Rodríguez, Merchán-Pérez, and DeFelipe describe a FIB-SEM protocol on mouse brain and validate candidate symmetric synapses as GABAergic with vesicular GABA transporter immunocytochemistry across ferrocyanide concentrations.
ocar.resolution: A low ferrocyanide concentration (0.1%) improved membrane visualization while still allowing unequivocal classification of synapses as asymmetric or symmetric.
ocar.future_work: The protocol is offered for studies that must keep type I/II identity while using volume EM; applying the same concentration series in other regions would test robustness.

summaries.beginner: Brain contacts come in two main looks: thick and thin. A common chemical used to make cell membranes easier to see in 3D electron microscopy can wash out that difference, and this paper finds a low dose that keeps both membranes and contact types clear.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy in 2024, Cano-Astorga and colleagues optimized FIB-SEM of mouse brain for classifying asymmetric versus symmetric synapses. Higher potassium ferrocyanide improved membranes but thinned postsynaptic densities, especially hurting symmetric-synapse identification. At 0.1% ferrocyanide, membranes were clearer and types remained unequivocal; VGAT immunocytochemistry was used to validate symmetric synapses as GABAergic.
summaries.advanced: The 0.1% figure is the concentration they demonstrate, not a universal optimum. Validation is on fixed mouse sections with VGAT; it supports GABAergic identity of identified symmetric synapses in this material, not a proof that every thin PSD is inhibitory in all regions. Catalog stages are sectioning and acquisition.

plain_language_summary: Brain contacts come in two main looks: thick and thin. A common chemical used to make cell membranes easier to see in 3D electron microscopy can wash out that difference, and this paper finds a low dose that keeps both membranes and contact types clear.

ocar.opportunity: 3D instance segmentation is needed in unlabeled microscopy modalities, but expert annotation is expensive, so adapting from labeled electron microscopy to unlabeled expansion microscopy would unlock new volumes.
ocar.challenge: Prior approaches either reuse generalist models or run image translation and segmentation as separate networks, which can add compute and miss joint constraints.
ocar.action: In IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics in 2023, Lauenburg, Lin, Zhang, and colleagues proposed CySGAN, a cyclic segmentation GAN that shares weights between translation and instance segmentation. At inference the translation layer can be removed. They trained with CycleGAN losses, source supervised losses, and self-supervised plus segmentation-based adversarial objectives on unlabeled target images.
ocar.resolution: On 3D neuronal nuclei segmentation from annotated EM to unlabeled ExM, CySGAN outperformed pretrained generalist models, feature-level domain-adaptation models, and sequential translation-then-segmentation baselines. They also released NucExM, a densely annotated ExM zebrafish brain nuclei dataset.
ocar.future_work: Code and NucExM are public. Testing CySGAN on other modality pairs would show whether the unified cyclic design remains superior outside EM-to-ExM nuclei.

summaries.beginner: Labeling every cell nucleus in a new kind of microscope image takes a long time. This method learns from already-labeled electron-microscope pictures and unlabeled expansion-microscope pictures at once, and it beat several older shortcuts.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE JBHI in 2023, Lauenburg et al. introduced CySGAN, which jointly performs image translation and 3D instance segmentation with weight sharing, adding no extra inference cost once translation is dropped. Benchmarked on EM-to-ExM neuronal nuclei, it outperformed generalist, feature-level adaptation, and sequential baselines. The authors released the annotated NucExM zebrafish dataset.
summaries.advanced: Outperformance is asserted without numeric scores in the abstract. The target task is nuclei in zebrafish ExM, not synapse segmentation. Domain adaptation still assumes related source/target structure; failures on more distant modalities are not characterized here.

plain_language_summary: Labeling every cell nucleus in a new kind of microscope image takes a long time. This method learns from already-labeled electron-microscope pictures and unlabeled expansion-microscope pictures at once, and it beat several older shortcuts.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric EM now yields large connectomes that can in principle be turned into biophysical simulations of every neuron, but insight requires simpler mathematical views of the wiring.
ocar.challenge: Detailed models have many parameters, so it is not obvious which connectivity features set circuit timescales or whether a network is feed-forward versus recurrent.
ocar.action: In Journal of Neuroscience in 2023, Borst and Leibold review two strategies: linear dynamical systems analysis and matrix reordering. They show how connectivity can create timescales longer than membrane constants and how reordering can reveal structural motifs.
ocar.resolution: Linear analysis predicts new time constants of information processing from connectivity. Matrix reordering can expose whether a circuit is strictly feed-forward or contains feedback. The viewpoint is a concise methods guide rather than a new dataset.
ocar.future_work: The authors present these tools as ways to extract insight from connectomics data; applying them systematically to newly released volumes would test the predicted timescales and motifs.

summaries.beginner: A giant wiring map is hard to think about one connection at a time. This article explains two math tricks: one for how slowly or quickly a network can respond, and one for rearranging the map so loops versus one-way chains become visible.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience in 2023, Borst and Leibold review linear dynamical systems analysis and matrix reordering for connectomes. Connectivity can generate timescales far longer than intrinsic membrane constants, and reordering can reveal feed-forward versus feedback motifs that are invisible in an arbitrary neuron numbering. The piece is a viewpoint on extracting function-relevant structure from wiring data.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/viewpoint, not a new reconstruction. Predictions about timescales assume linear(ized) dynamics. Motif visibility after reordering depends on the chosen permutation method. Catalog methods list network motifs; no specific organism or dataset is claimed.

plain_language_summary: A giant wiring map is hard to think about one connection at a time. This article explains two math tricks: one for how slowly or quickly a network can respond, and one for rearranging the map so loops versus one-way chains become visible.

ocar.opportunity: Mitochondria instance segmentation in large 3D EM volumes is a community bottleneck, and a shared challenge can compare methods on cortex-scale data rather than tiny crops.
ocar.challenge: Previous mitochondria datasets were small. Scoring can be too forgiving of false positives, and size-based instance grouping may not match biologically interesting mitochondria.
ocar.action: In IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging in 2023, Franco-Barranco, Lin, Jang, and many co-authors report the MitoEM challenge (IEEE-ISBI 2021) on two large 3D volumes from human and rat cortex, 1,986 times larger than previously used datasets. They summarize eight top methods plus baselines, corrected ground-truth errors after the challenge without changing ranking, and retrospectively redesigned the score.
ocar.resolution: 257 participants registered, 14 teams submitted, six joined the workshop. Several top methods compared favorably to the organizers’ baselines, but substantial errors remained for mitochondria with challenging morphologies. The new scoring system is meant to reflect correctness better; the challenge remains open with automatic evaluation.
ocar.future_work: Because hard morphologies remain unsolved, the benchmark stays open. Later submissions can be judged with the revised metric on the corrected labels.

summaries.beginner: This contest asked computers to outline every mitochondrion in two very large 3D electron-microscope blocks of cortex. The best entries beat simple baselines, but oddly shaped mitochondria still confuse the algorithms, so the contest stays open.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TMI in 2023, Franco-Barranco et al. present MitoEM: human and rat cortex volumes 1,986× larger than prior sets. Of 257 registrants, 14 teams submitted and six presented at the ISBI 2021 workshop. Post-challenge ground-truth fixes did not change ranking. A retrospective showed the original metric was permissive of false positives and poorly grouped instances by size; a new score is proposed. Hard morphologies remain error-prone.
summaries.advanced: Participant counts and the 1,986× size ratio are as stated; per-method scores are not in the abstract. Ranking invariance after GT correction is claimed globally, not instance-by-instance here. Volumes are human and rat cortex; organism tag is ‘other’. Segmentation and proofreading stages apply.

plain_language_summary: This contest asked computers to outline every mitochondrion in two very large 3D electron-microscope blocks of cortex. The best entries beat simple baselines, but oddly shaped mitochondria still confuse the algorithms, so the contest stays open.

ocar.opportunity: Globular bushy cells are central to timing in the cochlear nucleus, and volume EM can supply exact endbulb convergence, synaptic weights, and compartment surface areas for constrained models.
ocar.challenge: After decades of work, dendrite structure, afferent innervation, and synaptic integration of GBCs remain incompletely specified, so compartmental models have been underconstrained.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2023, Spirou, Kersting, Carr, and colleagues used volume EM to build synaptic maps of auditory-nerve axons and endbulbs with high-resolution dendrite, soma, and axon reconstructions, then exported them into biophysically detailed compartmental models driven by a standard cochlear transduction model.
ocar.resolution: Models predicted innervation profiles in which all endbulbs onto a GBC are subthreshold (coincidence detection) or one or two inputs are suprathreshold (mixed mode). They also ranked dendrite geometry, soma size, and axon-initial-segment length as contributors to threshold and response heterogeneity. Volume EM revealed new dendritic structures and dendrites that lack innervation.
ocar.future_work: The authors note missing cellular parameters that need new experiments and treat the pipeline as a template for other neuron classes, including predicted sound responses for in vivo tests.

summaries.beginner: Certain cells in the hearing pathway must keep the timing of sounds. This team measured their exact shape and incoming contacts with 3D electron microscopy, then simulated how those contacts could add up.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2023 bioRxiv preprint, Spirou and colleagues reconstructed globular bushy cells and their auditory-nerve endbulbs with volume EM and built constrained compartmental models. Simulations supported either all-subthreshold coincidence detection or mixed modes with one or two suprathreshold endbulbs, and they highlighted dendrite geometry, soma size, and AIS length as excitability knobs. Uninnervated dendrites and new dendritic structures were also observed.
summaries.advanced: Predicted modes are model outputs under stated constraints, not intracellular in vivo classifications in this abstract. No numerical convergence ratios appear here even though the text says maps ‘precisely specify’ them. Catalog stages include segmentation, infrastructure, and acquisition; organism is untagged.

plain_language_summary: Certain cells in the hearing pathway must keep the timing of sounds. This team measured their exact shape and incoming contacts with 3D electron microscopy, then simulated how those contacts could add up.

ocar.opportunity: Opponent inhibition is a common circuit motif, and the fly visual system is mapped well enough to pin synaptic, cellular, and network mechanisms of motion opponency onto identified cells.
ocar.challenge: In most systems the wiring and biophysics that generate opponency are unknown, and integrating large opposing conductances at a single stage would be expected to crush gain.
ocar.action: In Nature Neuroscience in 2023, Ammer, Serbe-Kamp, Mauss, Richter, Fendl, and Borst combined optogenetics, voltage and calcium imaging, connectomics, electrophysiology, and modeling in Drosophila.
ocar.resolution: A single cell type implements direction-selective, motion-opponent inhibition at three nested network levels via GluClα receptors, balanced with excitation in strength despite tenfold fewer synapses. Distributing the computation across consecutive levels counteracts gain loss from large opposing conductances. The architecture is proposed to keep selectivity high without sacrificing sensitivity in noise.
ocar.future_work: The nested-level account is a mechanistic proposal supported by this multimodal evidence; testing whether the same cell type’s roles generalize to other visual behaviors would extend the claim.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly motion circuits compare movement in opposite directions by using one kind of cell as a brake at several successive steps. Splitting that comparison across steps helps the circuit stay both picky and sensitive.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience in 2023, Ammer and colleagues show that one Drosophila visual cell type implements motion-opponent inhibition at three nested circuit levels through GluClα. Despite about tenfold fewer synapses, inhibition balances excitation. Electrophysiology and modeling suggest that spreading the computation across levels avoids the gain collapse expected from integrating large opposing conductances at once.
summaries.advanced: The ‘tenfold fewer synapses’ figure is as stated; other synapse counts are not given. Balance of inhibition and excitation is a strength comparison in this circuit, not a universal ratio. Nested levels operate at increasing spatiotemporal scales by the authors’ account. Catalog stage is graph analysis; methods in the row are empty even though the work is multimodal.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly motion circuits compare movement in opposite directions by using one kind of cell as a brake at several successive steps. Splitting that comparison across steps helps the circuit stay both picky and sensitive.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM can measure dendritic spine-head volumes as a proxy for synaptic weight, and comparing spines that share an axon and dendrite estimates how precisely plasticity stores information.
ocar.challenge: Connectomics produces more structural data than existing analyses can turn into information-theoretic storage capacity, and prior signal-detection estimates can be biased by overlapping states and outliers.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2023, Samavat, Bartol, Bromer, and colleagues introduced synaptic information storage capacity (SISC) from 3DEM, clustering non-overlapping spine-head volumes, and applied it in rat hippocampus after in vivo LTP, comparing CA1 stratum radiatum with dentate gyrus middle molecular layer.
ocar.resolution: CA1 radiatum spines occupied 24 distinguishable states (4.1 bits). Control dentate gyrus occupied 5 states (2 bits). Thirty minutes after LTP, dentate gyrus occupied 10 states (3 bits), lasting at least 2 hours, with a broader, nearly uniform distribution toward the theoretical SISC upper bound.
ocar.future_work: SISC is offered as a probe of plasticity in normal and diseased brains; applying it in additional regions and after other plasticity protocols would test how general the LTP-linked capacity increase is.

summaries.beginner: The size of a tiny spine on a brain cell is a clue to how strong that contact is. Counting how many distinct size groups exist estimates how much information a contact can store, and that number rose after a learning-related boost in part of the hippocampus.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2023 bioRxiv preprint, Samavat, Harris, Sejnowski, and colleagues define SISC from non-overlapping clusters of spine-head volumes in serial-section EM. Rat CA1 stratum radiatum showed 24 states (4.1 bits) versus 5 states (2 bits) in control dentate gyrus middle molecular layer. After in vivo LTP, dentate gyrus reached 10 states (3 bits) by 30 minutes, lasting at least 2 hours.
summaries.advanced: Bit values follow from log2 of distinguishable-state counts as reported (24, 5, 10 states). SISC assumes spine-head volume is well correlated with synaptic weight and that non-overlapping clusters are the right state definition. Shared axon–dendrite pairs are the biological motivation for precision; the abstract does not give a pairwise similarity statistic. Organism tag is ‘other’; the tissue is rat hippocampus. Sectioning/infrastructure stages match 3DEM.

plain_language_summary: The size of a tiny spine on a brain cell is a clue to how strong that contact is. Counting how many distinct size groups exist estimates how much information a contact can store, and that number rose after a learning-related boost in part of the hippocampus.

ocar.opportunity: Multiple synapse-resolution connectomes now exist beyond C. elegans, so one can ask whether structural statistics are shared across brain compartments and species.
ocar.challenge: Most prior topology work focused on individual C. elegans networks, leaving unclear whether small-worldness, modules, rich clubs, and degree tails are intrinsic to biological neural networks more generally.
ocar.action: In IEEE/ACM Transactions on Computational Biology and Bioinformatics in 2023, Zhao, Shao, Shi, He, and Gong collected nine synaptic-resolution connectomes including C. elegans and Drosophila larva and compared small-worldness, modularity, rich clubs, weight distributions, degree CCDFs, and subgraph significance profiles.
ocar.resolution: All nine networks showed small-world properties and modules, and all but the Drosophila larval visual system had rich clubs. Synaptic-strength distributions fit truncated power laws, while log-normal models fit degree CCDFs better than power laws. Significance profiles of small subgraphs placed the networks in the same superfamily.
ocar.future_work: Shared topology is interpreted as a formation principle; developmental or evolutionary tests of that principle are outside this comparative survey.

summaries.beginner: The authors compared nine detailed wiring maps from worms and flies. Despite coming from different animals and brain parts, the maps shared several network patterns, as if similar design rules were reused.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE/ACM Transactions on Computational Biology and Bioinformatics in 2023, Zhao, Shao, Shi, He, and Gong analyzed nine synapse-resolution connectomes including C. elegans. They report small-world structure and modules in all nine, and rich clubs in all except the Drosophila larval visual system. Synaptic-strength distributions fit truncated power laws, degree CCDFs fit log-normals better than power laws, and subgraph significance profiles placed the networks in the same superfamily.
summaries.advanced: ‘Nine connectomes’ are not named beyond C. elegans and the Drosophila larval visual exception. Truncated power-law and log-normal claims are distribution-class statements without reported exponents here. Superfamily membership is from subgraph SPs, a motif-significance signature, not proof of a shared generative mechanism. Datasets tagged: C. elegans and Drosophila larva.

plain_language_summary: The authors compared nine detailed wiring maps from worms and flies. Despite coming from different animals and brain parts, the maps shared several network patterns, as if similar design rules were reused.

ocar.opportunity: Ciona electron-microscopy connectomes still need synapse identification, and predicting neurotransmitter type from synapse appearance would add function to the wiring map where it was unknown.
ocar.challenge: Manual synapse classification is labor-intensive and expert-heavy, and relating synapse structure to cell type and transmitter is often difficult.
ocar.action: In Biological Imaging in 2022, Zhang, Shailja, Borba, Miao, and colleagues built a deep-learning workflow to detect synapses and predict neurotransmitter type in Ciona intestinalis EM, using class activation maps to highlight structural features.
ocar.resolution: The main result is differentiation of synapses by neurotransmitter type from EM structure, enabling transmitter predictions for Ciona neurons that were previously unknown. Class activation maps provided interpretable features tied to cell type and function. Code is on GitHub.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the workflow as a way to hasten connectome analysis; applying it to additional Ciona volumes would test transmitter predictions against independent biochemical labels where available.

summaries.beginner: In a sea squirt’s electron-microscope images, the team taught a computer to find contacts between nerve cells and to guess which chemical messenger each contact uses from how it looks. That guess is meant to add a chemical identity to a wiring map where many cells had none.
summaries.intermediate: In Biological Imaging in 2022, Zhang et al. trained a deep network to detect synapses and predict neurotransmitter type in Ciona EM. Class activation maps were used to interpret structural features by cell type and function. The approach yields transmitter predictions for Ciona neurons that lacked prior assignments.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not report accuracy, class list, or number of synapses. Transmitter identity is predicted from structure, not from direct chemical measurement in this description. Dataset tag is DS20 Ciona; organism is ‘other’.

plain_language_summary: In a sea squirt’s electron-microscope images, the team taught a computer to find contacts between nerve cells and to guess which chemical messenger each contact uses from how it looks. That guess is meant to add a chemical identity to a wiring map where many cells had none.

ocar.opportunity: A brain-wide Drosophila neuron-to-neuron connectome can be coarse-grained into connectivity-defined cell classes, giving a mesoscopic circuit that is still functionally interpretable.
ocar.challenge: Without a quantitative parts list at the cell-class level, systems-level questions about hubs, sources, destinations, and information flow remain tied to tens of thousands of individual neurons.
ocar.action: In Network Neuroscience in 2022, Mehta, Goldin, and Ascoli applied stochastic block modeling and spectral clustering so that neurons sharing connection-probability patterns form classes. They then related classes to neurotransmitters, birthtimes, morphology, spatial embedding, and functional anatomy, and used graph and random-walk analyses to label hubs, sources, and destinations.
ocar.resolution: Mutual information indicated that connectivity-based classes capture aspects missed by traditional schemes, including a dopaminergic interconnected core interpreted as a multisensory backbone. Other predicted pathways involved glutamatergic-dominant motor–optic links (possibly circadian), spatial orientation, fight-or-flight, and olfactory learning. Birthtimes mapped temporal change of the blueprint, including critical growth periods of pathways.
ocar.future_work: The authors offer experimentally testable hypotheses linking architecture to function; those hypotheses still need physiological tests.

summaries.beginner: Instead of naming fly brain cells only by shape or chemistry, this study groups them by who they connect to. The grouped map highlights a tightly linked dopamine core and several candidate communication routes.
summaries.intermediate: In Network Neuroscience in 2022, Mehta, Goldin, and Ascoli clustered a brain-wide Drosophila connectome with stochastic block models into connectivity-defined cell classes. Classes were compared with standard biomarkers via mutual information, then analyzed as hubs, sources, or destinations. They report a dopaminergic interconnected core, glutamatergic-dominant motor–optic connections, and birthtime-linked pathway growth periods.
summaries.advanced: Functional labels (multisensory integration, circadian, fight-or-flight, olfactory learning) are inferences from class composition and graph role, not new behavior experiments. Mutual information shows non-redundancy with traditional schemes, not superiority for all tasks. Catalog dimension is image-acquisition/preparation; the work is graph clustering on an existing connectome.

plain_language_summary: Instead of naming fly brain cells only by shape or chemistry, this study groups them by who they connect to. The grouped map highlights a tightly linked dopamine core and several candidate communication routes.

ocar.opportunity: An identified inhibitory olfactory local interneuron can be compared across hemispheres and individuals, turning neuronal variability from an annoyance into a measurable biological variable.
ocar.challenge: It has been unclear how much wiring varies within and between individuals, on what timescales, and with what function, even in systems with identified neurons.
ocar.action: In Science Advances in 2022, Chou, Yang, Huang, Liou, and colleagues used genetic labeling and electron-microscopy connectomics to map glomerular innervation of the identified inhibitory olfactory local interneuron TC-LN, including sexual dimorphism and mating-related changes.
ocar.resolution: TC-LN innervation patterns were extraordinarily variable. Innervation of VL2a, a glomerulus that processes food signals and modulates mating, was sexually dimorphic, influenced by female courtship experience, and correlated with food intake in mated females. Mating also changed TC-LN output connectivity onto specific local interneurons.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose that mating-associated TC-LN variability changes how food odor is read by an inhibitory network to modulate feeding—a hypothesis for causal tests.

summaries.beginner: Even a named cell type in the fly smell circuit does not wire the same way in every fly. In females, mating experience changed how that cell mixed into a food-odor region, in step with how much they ate.
summaries.intermediate: In Science Advances in 2022, Chou, Luo, Jefferis, and colleagues show that Drosophila TC-LN olfactory local interneurons vary strongly in glomerular innervation. VL2a innervation is sexually dimorphic, depends on female courtship experience, and correlates with food intake in mated females. Mating also altered TC-LN output onto specific local interneurons.
summaries.advanced: Variability is described as ‘extraordinary’ without a numeric dispersion statistic in the abstract. VL2a’s food/mating role is given as prior knowledge used to interpret the dimorphism. Correlation with food intake in mated females is not a proven causal circuit for feeding. Organism tag is empty; the animal is Drosophila. Method tag is electron microscopy plus genetic labeling.

plain_language_summary: Even a named cell type in the fly smell circuit does not wire the same way in every fly. In females, mating experience changed how that cell mixed into a food-odor region, in step with how much they ate.

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM segmentation now labels voxels at terabyte scale, but quantitative morphology and synaptic analysis still need skeletons, preferably in a high-performance language used for scientific computing.
ocar.challenge: Existing skeletonization and morphology tools are split across languages and environments, and they are hard to run on distributed cloud-scale zebrafish segmentations.
ocar.action: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics in 2022, Zhao, Wu, Turner, Bae, Vishwanathan, and Seung present RealNeuralNetworks.jl, a Julia package for sparse skeletonization, morphological analysis, and synaptic connectivity. They demonstrate distributed skeletonization of a large-scale zebrafish segmentation on Google Cloud, NBLAST clustering, and joint morphological–synaptic analysis.
ocar.resolution: The package is shown to be suitable for terabyte-scale EM segmentation datasets, combining skeletons, NBLAST similarity, and synaptic connectivity in one Julia environment.
ocar.future_work: The zebrafish demonstration is a feature illustration; broader adoption would depend on applying the same pipeline to other segmented volumes.

summaries.beginner: After a computer colors in every neuron in a huge electron-microscope stack, this Julia software traces stick-figure skeletons and compares their shapes and contacts. The authors ran it on a zebrafish brain dataset in the cloud.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics in 2022, Zhao, Wu, Turner, Bae, Vishwanathan, and Seung introduce RealNeuralNetworks.jl for skeletonization, morphology, and synaptic analysis of terabyte-scale 3D segmentations. They demonstrate distributed skeletonization of a large zebrafish electron-microscopy segmentation on Google Cloud. Neurons were clustered with NBLAST, and morphological similarity was combined with synaptic connectivity in one Julia environment.
summaries.advanced: ‘Suitable for terabyte-scale’ is demonstrated on one zebrafish dataset, not a timed benchmark table in the abstract. NBLAST clustering quality metrics are not reported here. Catalog datasets include DS15 zebrafish; method is electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: After a computer colors in every neuron in a huge electron-microscope stack, this Julia software traces stick-figure skeletons and compares their shapes and contacts. The authors ran it on a zebrafish brain dataset in the cloud.

ocar.opportunity: Feeding initiation in adult Drosophila is a discrete sensorimotor decision that can be mapped from gustatory sensory neurons to proboscis motor neurons at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: Taste and hunger both gate feeding, but the circuit that integrates those cues for proboscis extension was not fully reconstructed and tested neuron by neuron.
ocar.action: In eLife in 2022 (catalog journal field lists bioRxiv), Shiu, Sterne, Engert, Dickson, and Scott combined synaptic-resolution reconstruction with targeted genetic access to neurons in a gustatory sensorimotor pathway.
ocar.resolution: The circuit links sensory neurons to proboscis motor neurons through three intermediate layers; most pathway neurons were necessary and sufficient for sugar-driven proboscis extension. Hunger amplified the pathway at select second-order neurons. A bitter pathway inhibited premotor neurons, providing a local motif that weighs sugar against bitter.
ocar.future_work: The reconstruction explains flexible feeding initiation in this pathway; how the same logic extends to other feeding-related actions is left open.

summaries.beginner: The authors mapped the fly brain cells that decide whether to stick out the feeding tube when sugar is tasted. Hunger turns the volume up at an early step, and bitter taste hits the brakes just before movement.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife in 2022, Shiu, Scott, Dickson, and colleagues reconstruct an adult Drosophila feeding-initiation circuit from gustatory sensory neurons to proboscis motor neurons via three intermediate layers. Most identified neurons were necessary and sufficient for sugar-driven proboscis extension. Hunger acted at select second-order neurons; bitter inhibition converged on premotor neurons.
summaries.advanced: Necessity/sufficiency and sugar selectivity are stated for ‘most’ pathway neurons, not all. Hunger amplification is localized to select second-order cells; bitter inhibition to premotor cells—these are specific loci, not a global gain change. Catalog journal field says bioRxiv; DOI is eLife. Stage is graph analysis; organism is fly.

plain_language_summary: The authors mapped the fly brain cells that decide whether to stick out the feeding tube when sugar is tasted. Hunger turns the volume up at an early step, and bitter taste hits the brakes just before movement.

ocar.opportunity: A complete directed, weighted database of rat brainstem connections would support network analysis, disorder prediction, and simulation in a subdivision that is otherwise fragmented across papers.
ocar.challenge: Connectivity data are scattered in original tract-tracing reports, so building an analyzable brainstem connectome requires long-term metastudy and a software framework.
ocar.action: In Scientific Data in 2022, Schmitt, Eipert, Ruß, Beier, Kadir, and Horn released the brainstem connectome database collated from tract-tracing literature into neuroVIISAS, with access via tables, a web tool, and the framework. They analyzed global and local metrics, motifs, and communities, and modeled signal propagation through a somatosensory pathway relevant to multiple sclerosis.
ocar.resolution: The brainstem connectome is reported as a scale-free network with small-world connectivity. Louvain modularity and weighted stochastic block matching partially matched functions to connectivity. The resource is a metastudy of Rattus tracing, not a new EM volume.
ocar.future_work: The database is meant for ongoing analysis and modeling; users can extend it as new tracing studies appear.

summaries.beginner: This paper gathers decades of rat brainstem tracing studies into one directed connection list. The resulting network looks both locally clustered and globally hubby, and it can be used to simulate how signals travel.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Data in 2022, Schmitt and colleagues published a metastudy database of directed, weighted rat brainstem connections in neuroVIISAS. Graph analyses indicated scale-free, small-world structure, with community methods only partly aligning modules to known functions. They illustrate modeling on a somatosensory pathway affected in multiple sclerosis.
summaries.advanced: Scale-free and small-world labels are for this collated tract-tracing graph. Partial function–connectivity match is reported for Louvain and weighted SBM without a numeric agreement score here. Organism is rat (‘other’ tag). Stages include proofreading, infrastructure, graph analysis, and modeling.

plain_language_summary: This paper gathers decades of rat brainstem tracing studies into one directed connection list. The resulting network looks both locally clustered and globally hubby, and it can be used to simulate how signals travel.

ocar.opportunity: Knowing which neurons send monosynaptic input to genetically defined visual-cortex classes is a prerequisite for relating structure to visual function across the mouse brain.
