ocar.challenge: Brain-wide monosynaptic input maps to defined cell classes were limited by tracing efficiency and by the difficulty of quantifying target-, layer-, and class-specific differences at scale.
ocar.action: In Nature Neuroscience in 2021 (catalog journal field lists bioRxiv), Yao, Wang, Hirokawa, and Allen Institute colleagues optimized rabies tracing and applied it to mouse visual cortex to generate brain-wide monosynaptic input connectomes for genetically defined populations.
ocar.resolution: Maps showed quantitative target-, layer-, and cell-class-specific differences and supported ventral and dorsal visual streams plus continuously varying higher-area subnetworks. Intracortical feedforward and feedback via upper- versus lower-layer inputs recovered a visual-cortex hierarchy. Layer 6 neurons were assigned a new role in reciprocal interhemispheric connections.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the pipeline as scalable to other mouse cell populations; applying it beyond visual cortex would test how general the stream and hierarchy signatures are.

summaries.beginner: The team used a virus that jumps one connection backward to list the brain-wide inputs onto specific cell classes in mouse visual cortex. The lists recover known visual streams and a layered hierarchy, and they highlight layer 6 cells in cross-hemisphere talk.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience in 2021, Yao, Wang, Hirokawa, and Allen Institute colleagues report an optimized rabies pipeline for brain-wide monosynaptic inputs to genetically defined mouse visual-cortex neurons. Input maps differed by target, layer, and cell class and supported dorsal and ventral streams plus topographic higher-area subnetworks. A cortical hierarchy was recovered from upper- versus lower-layer feedforward and feedback, and layer 6 was implicated in reciprocal interhemispheric connectivity.
summaries.advanced: Catalog journal is listed as bioRxiv; DOI is Nature Neuroscience 2021. ‘New role’ for layer 6 is relative to prior tracing literature as framed here, not a physiological demonstration in this abstract. Quantities are described as target/layer/class-specific without numeric projection strengths in the abstract. Organism is mouse; stages are proofreading and graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: The team used a virus that jumps one connection backward to list the brain-wide inputs onto specific cell classes in mouse visual cortex. The lists recover known visual streams and a layered hierarchy, and they highlight layer 6 cells in cross-hemisphere talk.

ocar.opportunity: Unmyelinated axons are the most common fibers but are rarely quantified at scale, so automated instance segmentation from transmission EM would fill a biased gap in peripheral and central connectomes.
ocar.challenge: Manual counting becomes unmanageable as axon numbers grow, and existing characterizations have ignored unmyelinated fibers.
ocar.action: In Scientific Reports in 2021, Plebani, Biscola, Havton, Rajwa, and colleagues annotated all unmyelinated axons in rat vagus and pelvic-nerve TEM images and trained a deep instance-segmentation network, testing stand-alone versus expert-in-the-loop use and different training strategies.
ocar.resolution: Stand-alone instance-level F1 scores were between 0.7 and 0.9 on various test images. In the hybrid setting, expert annotation labor fell by 80%. They present this as a first prototype high-throughput pipeline for unmyelinated fibers.
ocar.future_work: The authors hope the pipeline will enable scale characterization of unmyelinated axons in both PNS and CNS; additional nerves and species would test the F1 range.

summaries.beginner: Most nerve fibers lack a myelin wrapper and are tedious to outline by hand. A computer trained on rat nerve electron-microscope pictures found those fibers with useful accuracy and cut expert drawing time by four-fifths when a person stayed in the loop.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports in 2021, Plebani et al. trained a deep instance-segmentation network on fully annotated unmyelinated axons in rat vagus and pelvic-nerve TEM. Stand-alone F1 was 0.7–0.9 depending on the test image; an expert-in-the-loop mode reduced annotation labor by 80%. They frame the work as a prototype for high-throughput unmyelinated-fiber morphometry.
summaries.advanced: F1 is instance-level and image-dependent (0.7–0.9), not a single dataset-wide score. The 80% labor cut is for the hybrid setting, not fully automatic production. Tissue is rat peripheral nerve TEM, not brain connectome EM. Catalog stages include acquisition, segmentation, and proofreading.

plain_language_summary: Most nerve fibers lack a myelin wrapper and are tedious to outline by hand. A computer trained on rat nerve electron-microscope pictures found those fibers with useful accuracy and cut expert drawing time by four-fifths when a person stayed in the loop.

ocar.opportunity: Petascale computers can, in principle, run modern machine-learning segmentation over large EM volumes so that dendritic spines—and thus many synapses—can be extracted for morphology at population scale.
ocar.challenge: Even with better automatic segmentation, extracting neuronal and synaptic profiles from connectomic volumes is hard to scale, limiting synapse-morphology studies to small fields of view.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2021, Wildenberg, Li, Badalamente, Uram, Ferrier, and Kasthuri segmented a 0.6 terabyte EM dataset with state-of-the-art machine learning on a substantial fraction of Argonne’s 11.69 petaFLOPs Theta supercomputer, using an iterative human–machine feedback pipeline, then algorithmically extracted dendritic spines.
ocar.resolution: The pipeline produced segmentation in time frames aimed at making connectomics more routine for synapse-morphology questions, and demonstrated algorithmic spine extraction for morphological analysis. The authors emphasize turnaround and population-level views of synapses from different neurons.
ocar.future_work: They expect large-compute segmentation to accelerate biology on individual datasets; applying the same loop to additional volumes would test whether accuracy gains from more compute-intensive algorithms hold.

summaries.beginner: Mapping tiny spines on neurons in a huge electron-microscope stack takes more computing than a lab workstation can offer. This team ran the job on a supercomputer, with people correcting the machine, then automatically pulled out spines for measurement.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2021 bioRxiv preprint, Wildenberg, Kasthuri, and colleagues used Argonne’s Theta supercomputer (11.69 petaFLOPs) to segment a 0.6 TB EM volume with contemporary ML methods and iterative human feedback. They then extracted dendritic spines algorithmically for morphology. The goal is faster, population-scale synapse morphometry from connectomic EM.
summaries.advanced: 0.6 TB and 11.69 petaFLOPs are the stated dataset and machine figures; no Dice or VI scores appear in the abstract. ‘Accurate segmentation’ is the pipeline’s aim, not a reported metric here. Organism is untagged. Stages are segmentation and infrastructure.

plain_language_summary: Mapping tiny spines on neurons in a huge electron-microscope stack takes more computing than a lab workstation can offer. This team ran the job on a supercomputer, with people correcting the machine, then automatically pulled out spines for measurement.

ocar.opportunity: Neocortical function depends on stereotyped synaptic targeting of cell types and even of subcellular domains, so developmental rules that build that specificity are a core circuit question.
ocar.challenge: Many targeting studies confound cell-type preference with laminar targeting because axons aim at layers. In cortex, cell bodies and processes of many types intermingle in each layer, which makes selective synapse formation harder to explain and to measure.
ocar.action: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits in 2021, Gutman-Wei and Brown review mechanisms of target selectivity in developing neocortex—axonal/dendritic guidance, fine-scale morphogenesis, lineage, activity, and intercellular molecules—and highlight recent progress, challenges, and gaps specific to intracortical connectivity.
ocar.resolution: The review organizes how multiple mechanisms can yield cell-type-biased and domain-specific synapses among intermingled cortical neurons, notes links to neurodevelopmental disorders, and flags current gaps in understanding cortical synapse specificity.
ocar.future_work: The authors explicitly call out remaining gaps in determinants of stereotyped intracortical connectivity as the agenda for the field.

summaries.beginner: In the cortex, many cell types sit mixed together, yet they still connect in a reliable pattern, even to particular parts of a partner cell. This review explains what is known about how those choices are made while the circuit is wiring up.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits in 2021, Gutman-Wei and Brown review how developing neocortical circuits select synaptic partners by cell type and by subcellular domain. They contrast cortex, where many types intermingle in each layer, with systems in which targeting can be explained by laminar choice. Mechanisms surveyed include guidance, morphogenesis, lineage, activity, and molecular cues, including links to neurodevelopmental disorders, plus remaining gaps in intracortical specificity.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new connectome or causal screen. Mechanisms are compiled from the literature; no new numeric selectivity indices are reported. Axis is biological application / cell-types. Organism and dataset tags are empty.

plain_language_summary: In the cortex, many cell types sit mixed together, yet they still connect in a reliable pattern, even to particular parts of a partner cell. This review explains what is known about how those choices are made while the circuit is wiring up.

ocar.opportunity: Single-cell-type perturbations in a Drosophila larva mechanosensory circuit, read out at synaptic resolution, can show how identified cells contribute to assembly and function.
ocar.challenge: General principles of wiring specificity are hard to extract from one reconstruction; comparative connectomics after defined perturbations is still rare.
ocar.action: In Current Biology in 2021, Donà and Jefferis highlight a study that perturbs a specific cell type and measures effects on larval mechanosensory circuit assembly and function with synaptic-resolution connectomics.
ocar.resolution: The highlighted work paves the way for using comparative connectomics to find general rules of developmental wiring specificity.
ocar.future_work: As a dispatch, the piece points to comparative connectomics of perturbed circuits as the method to generalize beyond this mechanosensory example.

summaries.beginner: This short commentary describes a study that removed or changed one cell type in a young fruit-fly touch circuit and then remapped the wiring. That approach can reveal rules for how circuits are built.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology in 2021, Donà and Jefferis discuss a synaptic-resolution study of how single cell-type perturbations alter assembly and function of a Drosophila melanogaster larva mechanosensory circuit. The dispatch frames that work as comparative connectomics. The aim is to extract general principles of developmental wiring specificity from identified-cell perturbations.
summaries.advanced: This is a preview/dispatch (abstract 340 characters), not the primary reconstruction. Findings of the underlying study are not quantified here. Organism is fly; axis is biological application.

plain_language_summary: This short commentary describes a study that removed or changed one cell type in a young fruit-fly touch circuit and then remapped the wiring. That approach can reveal rules for how circuits are built.

ocar.opportunity: Neuronal nuclei segmentation at sub-cubic-millimeter scale would let lineage and expression studies move beyond tiny volumes with fewer than 500 nuclei.
ocar.challenge: Prior neuronal-nuclei datasets were usually smaller than 10⁻³ mm³, hiding diversity of appearance and density in large brain regions.
ocar.action: At MICCAI in 2021, Lin, Wei, Petkova, Wu, and colleagues released NucMM: a 0.1 mm³ EM volume of nearly the entire zebrafish brain (~170,000 nuclei) and a 0.25 mm³ micro-CT mouse visual-cortex volume (~7,000 nuclei). They quantified new challenges statistically and proposed a hybrid-representation model combining foreground, contour, and signed distance transforms.
ocar.resolution: Benchmarks on NucMM showed the hybrid model significantly outperformed state-of-the-art nuclei segmentation methods. Code and data were released.
ocar.future_work: Public NucMM enables further method comparison; generalizing the hybrid representation beyond these two volumes is the obvious follow-on.

summaries.beginner: The authors published two huge, fully labeled 3D pictures of cell nuclei: one almost a whole zebrafish brain and one a piece of mouse visual cortex. Their computer method, which mixes several ways of drawing each nucleus, beat existing tools on this harder test.
summaries.intermediate: At MICCAI in 2021, Lin et al. introduced NucMM: ~170,000 nuclei in 0.1 mm³ zebrafish EM and ~7,000 nuclei in 0.25 mm³ mouse visual-cortex micro-CT. Scale and dual modalities revealed diverse nuclear appearance and density. A hybrid mask–contour–distance model significantly outperformed prior nuclei segmentation methods; code and data are public.
summaries.advanced: ‘Significantly outperformed’ has no numeric metric in the abstract. EM and uCT challenges differ; a single hybrid model is claimed to handle both. Dataset tags include MICrONS and zebrafish; the mouse volume is described as part of visual cortex via micro-CT, not as the MICrONS EM volume.

plain_language_summary: The authors published two huge, fully labeled 3D pictures of cell nuclei: one almost a whole zebrafish brain and one a piece of mouse visual cortex. Their computer method, which mixes several ways of drawing each nucleus, beat existing tools on this harder test.

ocar.opportunity: Human MRI connectomes of prefrontal cortex can be interpreted more safely if they are checked against monosynaptic tracing in non-human primates, the historical gold standard for hard-wired pathways.
ocar.challenge: A key question is how well MRI-derived networks and hubs match the axonal trajectories and terminals first described by anatomy, especially given species and scale differences.
ocar.action: In Neuropsychopharmacology in 2021, Haber, Liu, Seidlitz, and Bullmore review monosynaptic PFC connections in non-human primates region by region, then compare that anatomy with MRI structural/functional connectivity and graph-theoretic hubs, modules, and integration in humans, using concrete examples.
ocar.resolution: The review argues that primate tracing can directly inform which prefrontal nodes, hubs, and edges in human MRI maps correspond to plausible anatomical pathways to cortex and subcortex.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a translation framework; new tracing or higher-resolution MRI would still be needed to close remaining mismatches.

summaries.beginner: Brain scans estimate how prefrontal regions talk, but they do not see single fibers. This review lines those estimates up with gold-standard tracing in monkeys so human maps can be read more cautiously.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuropsychopharmacology in 2021, Haber, Liu, Seidlitz, and Bullmore compare primate monosynaptic prefrontal tracing with human MRI connectomics and graph metrics. They outline prefrontal pathways region by region from cells of origin through axon trajectories to terminals. Examples show how that anatomy can constrain interpretation of MRI nodes, hubs, and edges in the human prefrontal connectome.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new tract-tracing or MRI dataset. Alignment between scales is conceptual and example-driven. Catalog stages are proofreading and graph analysis; organism tag is empty (primate anatomy versus human imaging).

plain_language_summary: Brain scans estimate how prefrontal regions talk, but they do not see single fibers. This review lines those estimates up with gold-standard tracing in monkeys so human maps can be read more cautiously.

ocar.opportunity: Miniature insects retain complex brains with thousands of neurons at body sizes comparable to unicellular organisms, so they could shrink the cost of complete circuit mapping relative to fly, fish, or mouse.
ocar.challenge: Human-brain research leans on a small set of models whose brains are still large and expensive to map completely; adding smaller insects needs a clear scientific rationale.
ocar.action: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2021, Makarova, Polilov, and Chklovskii argue for adding miniature insects to the model-organism collection, stressing identifiable neurons, connectome stereotypy, and evolutionary insight into brain design.
ocar.resolution: They propose that the smallest insects keep insect-style identified neurons and stereotyped connectomes while being easier to map, and that their brains illuminate evolution of compact designs.
ocar.future_work: The article is a prospectus: actual miniature-insect connectomes would be required to cash the promised cost and speed gains.

summaries.beginner: Some insects are almost as small as a single cell yet still have brains with thousands of neurons. The authors argue that mapping those tiny brains could teach us brain design faster and cheaper than working only in flies or mice.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2021, Makarova, Polilov, and Chklovskii propose miniature insects as connectomic models. Despite body sizes comparable to unicellular organisms, these insects retain complex brains with thousands of neurons, identified cells, and stereotyped wiring. The authors argue such brains should be cheaper to map than fly, fish, or mouse brains while still informing the evolution of compact brain designs.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/proposal, not a reconstruction. ‘Thousands of neurons’ is the scale they cite, not a counted connectome here. Catalog datasets list C. elegans and zebrafish and organism fly—the argument is comparative, not an analysis of those volumes.

plain_language_summary: Some insects are almost as small as a single cell yet still have brains with thousands of neurons. The authors argue that mapping those tiny brains could teach us brain design faster and cheaper than working only in flies or mice.

ocar.opportunity: A full connectome plus a multimodal cellular atlas of the young Platynereis worm now make it possible to compare core circuits of an ancestral-style bilaterian brain with other animals.
ocar.challenge: What constituted the first bilaterian brain’s core circuits, and how they relate to diverse modern brains, has been hard to ground without cellular-resolution maps in a slowly evolving marine annelid.
ocar.action: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2021, Arendt, Quintana Urzainqui, and Vergara synthesize Platynereis resources—the full connectome and a gene-expression plus ultrastructure atlas—into a comparative neuroanatomy argument.
ocar.resolution: They propose a composite ancestral bilaterian brain: the anterior end of a circular CNS fused to a sensory-neurosecretory apical system, with lhx6-arx-dlx chemosensory circuits giving rise to associative centers in later lineages.
ocar.future_work: The composite-core hypothesis is a comparative interpretation to be tested with additional spiralian and deuterostome cellular atlases.

summaries.beginner: A small marine worm now has a complete wiring map and a cell-by-cell atlas. Comparing those to other animals, the authors suggest the first complex brains were stitched from a ring-like nerve cord plus a sensory tip.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2021, Arendt, Quintana Urzainqui, and Vergara use the Platynereis dumerilii larval connectome and a multimodal cellular atlas to reconstruct ancestral bilaterian brain organization. They propose that an anterior circular central nervous system fused with a sensory-neurosecretory apical system. lhx6-arx-dlx chemosensory circuits are highlighted as precursors of associative centers in later lineages.
summaries.advanced: This is a synthesis/opinion grounded in named Platynereis resources, not a methods paper. The ancestral reconstruction is comparative inference. Dataset tag is DS22 Platynereis; stage is acquisition; organism is ‘other’.

plain_language_summary: A small marine worm now has a complete wiring map and a cell-by-cell atlas. Comparing those to other animals, the authors suggest the first complex brains were stitched from a ring-like nerve cord plus a sensory tip.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian circuits span synapses to whole brain, so a clearing method that preserves ultrastructure could let the same neurons be followed from light-microscopy overview into electron-microscopy synapses.
ocar.challenge: Multi-scale imaging usually breaks continuity because clearing, labeling, and EM are hard to chain without destroying nanometer structure.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2021, Furuta, Yamauchi, Okamoto, and colleagues coupled successive light and electron microscopy with ScaleSF, an ultrastructure-preserving clearing method, covering macroscopic, mesoscopic, microscopic, and EM nanoscale views.
ocar.resolution: Applied to mouse striatofugal, mouse callosal, and marmoset corticostriatal projections, the pipeline allowed simultaneous interrogation of circuit structure and synaptic connectivity in a targeted way, integrating information from brain to synapse.
ocar.future_work: The authors expect the approach to advance brain-wide connectivity studies by expanding object scales; more pathways and species would test how routine the LM/EM handoff can become.

summaries.beginner: The same nerve pathway is hard to see both as a whole-brain route and as individual contacts. A clearing recipe that still works for electron microscopy let the team zoom from mouse or marmoset overview down to synapses without losing the cells they started with.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2021 bioRxiv preprint, Furuta, Yamauchi, Okamoto, Hioki, and colleagues combine ScaleSF clearing with successive light and electron microscopy from whole brain to synapses. The pipeline covers macroscopic, mesoscopic, microscopic, and nanoscopic views while preserving ultrastructure. They demonstrate it on mouse striatofugal, mouse callosal, and marmoset corticostriatal projection systems.
summaries.advanced: Demonstration is on three projection systems in mouse and marmoset; it is a methods feasibility claim, not a full connectome. No resolution numbers beyond the four named scales appear in the abstract. Organism tag is mouse; marmoset is also in the abstract. Method tag is electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: The same nerve pathway is hard to see both as a whole-brain route and as individual contacts. A clearing recipe that still works for electron microscopy let the team zoom from mouse or marmoset overview down to synapses without losing the cells they started with.

ocar.opportunity: Combining neuroimaging with genetically informative designs can link molecular variation to the structural and functional human connectome.
ocar.challenge: No single genetic design answers how genes shape connectivity; heritability, variant association, and transcription–imaging spatial correlation each have different strengths and limits.
ocar.action: In NeuroImage in 2021, Arnatkevičiūtė, Fulcher, Bellgrove, and Fornito review three frameworks: twin heritability, DNA-variant association, and integration of imaging phenotypes with transcriptional atlases, summarizing discoveries and limitations.
ocar.resolution: Converging evidence indicates anatomical connectivity is under stronger genetic influence than functional connectivity, and that genetic influence is regionally uneven. They also discuss how imaging genetics can inform brain dysfunction in clinical disorders.
ocar.future_work: The review maps a research program; stronger causal links still require designs that combine these three frameworks with clinical cohorts.

summaries.beginner: This review asks how genes help set the pattern of human brain wiring and activity. Anatomy looks more heritable than functional coupling, and some regions are under tighter genetic control than others.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage in 2021, Arnatkevičiūtė, Fulcher, Bellgrove, and Fornito review twin, variant-association, and transcription-atlas approaches to the genetics of human brain networks. They conclude that structural connectivity is under stronger genetic influence than functional connectivity. Genetic effects are described as non-uniform across regions and connections, with implications for clinical imaging genetics.
summaries.advanced: Conclusions are syntheses of the literature, not a new cohort analysis. ‘Stronger genetic influence’ on anatomy versus function is the review’s converging claim; effect sizes are not given here. Catalog stage is infrastructure; organism tag is empty (human imaging genetics).

plain_language_summary: This review asks how genes help set the pattern of human brain wiring and activity. Anatomy looks more heritable than functional coupling, and some regions are under tighter genetic control than others.

ocar.opportunity: If connectomes predict physiology and behavior in health, mapping how synapses and circuit topologies change in disease—pathoconnectomics—could identify therapeutic targets.
ocar.challenge: Disease-corrupted network synaptology had not been mapped at connectome resolution for a degenerating retina, so neuron-by-neuron responses to lost network components were unknown.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2020, Pfeiffer, Anderson, Dahal, Garcia, and colleagues generated a retinal pathoconnectome from tissue with photoreceptor degeneration and compared rod-pathway connectivity and neurite sprouting to healthy topology.
ocar.resolution: They observed aberrant rod-network connectivity and novel synapses from neurite sprouting. These observations are offered as principles of how neurons respond to loss of network components, extendable to other neurodegenerative diseases.
ocar.future_work: The authors present this as the first pathoconnectome and a template for other degenerations; additional stages of disease would test which rewiring events are early versus late.

summaries.beginner: When light-sensing cells die in the retina, remaining cells do not simply go quiet—they form odd new contacts. This first disease-focused wiring map documents those mistaken connections.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Pfeiffer, Anderson, Dahal, Marc, Jones, and colleagues report a retinal pathoconnectome after photoreceptor degeneration. They find aberrant rod-pathway connectivity and novel synapses arising from neurite sprouting. The map is framed as the first pathoconnectome and as a template for how neurons respond when network components are lost.
summaries.advanced: ‘First pathoconnectome’ is the authors’ claim for this retinal degeneration volume. No synapse counts are in the abstract. Dataset tag is DS09/DS10 mouse retina; organism is mouse. Stage is graph analysis. Therapeutic-target language is prospective.

plain_language_summary: When light-sensing cells die in the retina, remaining cells do not simply go quiet—they form odd new contacts. This first disease-focused wiring map documents those mistaken connections.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans remains the only metazoan with a complete cell lineage, sequenced genome, and connectome from the same tradition, so it is a living archive of how neurodevelopment can be solved molecularly.
ocar.challenge: The field has grown from early visionaries to a large community; newcomers need a synthesis from neuron generation through navigation and connectivity, including newer topics such as glia, sex differences, and plasticity.
ocar.action: In Journal of Neurogenetics in 2020, Rapti reviews mechanisms of C. elegans neurodevelopment, explicitly connecting current work to Brenner, Sulston, and colleagues, and highlighting glia, sexual dimorphism, and developmental plasticity.
ocar.resolution: The perspective summarizes how neural components are generated, diversified, guided, and wired, and argues that multifaceted worm studies still convert genes into cell function and behavior while generating new questions.
ocar.future_work: Rapti frames emerging questions—especially glia, dimorphism, and plasticity—as the next discovery space built on the classic lineage and connectome.

summaries.beginner: This essay retells how the tiny worm became a map of brain development, from the first complete cell family tree and wiring diagram to newer work on support cells, sex differences, and flexible wiring. It is a guided tour for readers entering that still-growing field.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neurogenetics in 2020, Rapti reviews C. elegans neurodevelopment from lineage and diversification through axon navigation and connectivity. Modern results are tied back to Brenner, Sulston, and colleagues. Highlights include glia biology, sexual dimorphism, and plasticity, arguing that gene-to-behavior studies in this system still generate mechanistic questions.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective/review, not primary mapping. Dataset tag is DS01 C. elegans. No new numeric connectome statistics are reported.

plain_language_summary: This essay retells how the tiny worm became a map of brain development, from the first complete cell family tree and wiring diagram to newer work on support cells, sex differences, and flexible wiring. It is a guided tour for readers entering that still-growing field.

ocar.opportunity: Larval and adult Drosophila now have cell-type, connectome, and synaptome resources that could be queried together if they lived in one executable environment.
ocar.challenge: Fly brain data are split across databases and tables, making it slow to compare models across labs, developmental stages, and datasets or to attach physiology and genetics to wiring.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2020, Lazar, Liu, Turkcan, and Zhou introduce FlyBrainLab, an interactive open-source environment that integrates neuroanatomy, neurogenetics, electrophysiology, and executable circuit models, with UI, utility libraries for graphs, and circuit libraries for central complex and olfactory systems, plus molecular-transduction libraries for vision and olfaction.
ocar.resolution: The platform is positioned to turn disparate fly resources into a structured, executable circuit repository, supporting 3D exploration, model comparison, and biological validation of circuits in one place.
ocar.future_work: FlyBrainLab is infrastructure; its payoff depends on community models and on using sensory libraries plus activity data to discover circuit function beyond the connectome alone.

summaries.beginner: Fly brain data now include wiring, synapses, genes, and recordings, but they live in different places. FlyBrainLab puts them in one interactive workspace so a circuit you see can also be run as a model.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Lazar, Liu, Turkcan, and Zhou present FlyBrainLab, an open interactive environment that unifies Drosophila connectome and synaptome data with models, genetics, and electrophysiology. Utility libraries untangle graphs from raw connectivity, and circuit libraries cover the central complex and early olfaction in adult and larva. Additional libraries address visual and olfactory molecular transduction as entry points beyond the connectome alone.
summaries.advanced: This is a software/infrastructure paper, not a new connectome. Claims of accelerating discovery are prospective. Catalog stages are infrastructure, graph analysis, and modeling; organism is fly.

plain_language_summary: Fly brain data now include wiring, synapses, genes, and recordings, but they live in different places. FlyBrainLab puts them in one interactive workspace so a circuit you see can also be run as a model.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans connectome documents abundant gap junctions, and 25 innexin genes with dynamic expression offer a genetic handle on electrical synapses in a complete nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Roles of gap junctions beyond fast bidirectional coupling—especially in circuit formation, function, and stress—were scattered and needed a unified view.
ocar.action: In Biology Open in 2020, Jin, Park, Lyu, and Jin review historical and new findings on gap junctions and innexins in the worm nervous system, including non-neuronal tissues.
ocar.resolution: Recent work shows innexins regulate multiple processes in neural-circuit formation and function in both normal and stress conditions. The review highlights diverse roles of gap junctions and innexins as a contribution to understanding electrical synapses in all animals.
ocar.future_work: The authors treat worm innexin biology as a source of general principles still being expanded under stress and developmental conditions.

summaries.beginner: Worms, like other animals, have direct electrical pores between cells as well as chemical contacts. This review gathers how those pores, built from innexin proteins, help build and run circuits, including under stress.
summaries.intermediate: In Biology Open in 2020, Jin, Park, Lyu, and Jin review gap junctions in C. elegans, including their abundance in the connectome and 25 innexin genes with spatial and temporal expression. Recent findings assign innexins roles in circuit formation, function, and stress, in neurons and non-neuronal tissues. The authors argue these worm studies inform electrical-synapse biology in other animals.
summaries.advanced: This is a review. ‘Vast number’ of gap junctions and ‘25 innexin genes’ are as stated. Dataset tag is DS01 C. elegans. No new EM quantification is presented.

plain_language_summary: Worms, like other animals, have direct electrical pores between cells as well as chemical contacts. This review gathers how those pores, built from innexin proteins, help build and run circuits, including under stress.

ocar.opportunity: An open anterograde/retrograde tracing repository for the common marmoset now supports a systematic mesoscale cortico-cortical connectome analysis in a primate model.
ocar.challenge: Global efforts to relate behavior and perturbations to wiring need accurate white-matter maps in model organisms; marmoset network architecture had not been charted with the same topological toolkit used in other species.
ocar.action: In Network Neuroscience in 2020, Liu, Zheng, and Mišić analyzed the Marmoset Brain Architecture Project tracing data, quantifying path length, community structure, connective core, motifs, and cavities.
ocar.resolution: The network showed multiple non-random attributes balancing segregation and integration: near-minimal path length, multiscale communities, a connective core, unique motif composition, and multiple cavities. Findings aligned with reports across species, scales, and methods, suggesting shared organizational principles.
ocar.future_work: The analysis is offered as a foundation for future anatomical, functional, and behavioral marmoset studies.

summaries.beginner: Using public tracing maps of the marmoset monkey cortex, the authors show the network is both clumpy and globally well linked, with a densely connected core. Similar patterns have been reported in other animals, suggesting shared design rules.
summaries.intermediate: In Network Neuroscience in 2020, Liu, Zheng, and Mišić chart the mesoscale marmoset cortico-cortical connectome from the Marmoset Brain Architecture Project. They report near-minimal path length, multiscale community structure, a connective core, distinctive motifs, and cavities. These attributes are interpreted as a segregation–integration balance also reported across other species, scales, and reconstruction methods.
summaries.advanced: Topology is from directed tracing-based cortico-cortical graphs, not EM. ‘Near-minimal path length’ and ‘unique motif composition’ are not numerically specified in the abstract. Catalog stages are proofreading and graph analysis; organism tag is empty (marmoset).

plain_language_summary: Using public tracing maps of the marmoset monkey cortex, the authors show the network is both clumpy and globally well linked, with a densely connected core. Similar patterns have been reported in other animals, suggesting shared design rules.

ocar.opportunity: Large EM volumes of brain slices can be turned into 3D neuron visualizations on supercomputers if community tools are scaled with minimal source changes and can start during acquisition.
ocar.challenge: EM processing pipelines are often lab-specific, hard to run from workstation to supercomputer, and poorly composable as live, database-triggered workflows.
ocar.action: At the 2020 XLOOP workshop, Vescovi, Li, Kinnison, Keçeli, Salim, Kasthuri, Uram, and Ferrier present a modular, scalable software pipeline wrapping community EM packages, tested on workstation, cluster, and supercomputer, with Balsam-database workflows triggerable during acquisition.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate end-to-end segmentation of a large EM volume on a supercomputer and describe integration changes needed to scale existing codes. Modularity is intended so groups can swap step-specific tools without breaking the workflow.
ocar.future_work: The pipeline is a template for automated HPC EM processing; additional front ends and finer-grained execution control are mentioned as supported directions.

summaries.beginner: Turning a mountain of electron-microscope pictures into 3D neurons usually means stitching together many lab programs. This team wrapped those programs so they run from a desktop up to a supercomputer, even while the microscope is still collecting data.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 large-scale experiment-in-the-loop computing workshop paper, Vescovi, Li, Kinnison, Kasthuri, Uram, Ferrier, and colleagues describe a modular HPC pipeline for electron-microscopy connectomics. Community tools are scaled with minimal source changes and were tested on a workstation, a cluster, and a supercomputer. They demonstrate end-to-end segmentation of a large volume, with Balsam-triggered workflows that can start during acquisition.
summaries.advanced: No volume size, runtime, or accuracy metrics appear in the abstract. Success is demonstrated as engineering scalability, not a new biological reconstruction. Stages are acquisition, segmentation, and infrastructure; method is electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: Turning a mountain of electron-microscope pictures into 3D neurons usually means stitching together many lab programs. This team wrapped those programs so they run from a desktop up to a supercomputer, even while the microscope is still collecting data.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian cortices differ in size, cytology, and phylogeny, yet may still share wiring rules that link physical distance, cell architecture, and connections.
ocar.challenge: Intricate interareal wiring plus large species differences make it hard to separate species-specific patterns from a mammalian blueprint.
ocar.action: In PLoS Biology in 2019, Goulas, Majka, Rosa, and Hilgetag compared mouse, cat, marmoset, and macaque cortices, relating existence of connections and laminar origins to cytoarchitectonic gradients versus the rostrocaudal axis, and identifying network cores.
ocar.resolution: Connection existence related to cytology beyond distance, more weakly in mouse and marmoset. Laminar origin tracked cytoarchitectonic gradients, not the rostrocaudal axis, allowing extrapolation of that feature toward humans. All connectomes had a network core, displaced toward less neuronally dense cortex in cat and macaque, with possible functional and vulnerability consequences.
ocar.future_work: The blueprint is offered as a mix of conserved and species-specific links among connectional, physical, and cytological dimensions, possibly reflecting conserved cellular mechanisms.

summaries.beginner: Comparing cortical wiring maps from mouse, cat, and two monkeys, the authors find shared rules: how packed the cells are helps predict who connects to whom. A densely linked core sits in different places depending on the species.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology in 2019, Goulas et al. relate interareal connectivity in mouse, cat, marmoset, and macaque to distance and cytoarchitecture. Cytology predicts connection existence beyond distance (attenuated in mouse and marmoset). Laminar origins follow cytoarchitectonic gradients rather than the rostrocaudal axis. Network cores exist in all four, shifting toward less neuron-dense cortex in cat and macaque.
summaries.advanced: Extrapolation of laminar-origin principles to humans is an inference from gradient linkage, not a human tracing dataset. Core ‘displacement’ and vulnerability are interpretive. Catalog organism is mouse; the study is explicitly four-species. Stages are preparation and infrastructure.

plain_language_summary: Comparing cortical wiring maps from mouse, cat, and two monkeys, the authors find shared rules: how packed the cells are helps predict who connects to whom. A densely linked core sits in different places depending on the species.

ocar.opportunity: A cellular-resolution atlas of the 6 dpf larval zebrafish brain would provide ground truth for later synapse-scale EM and a public map from neuron morphology to areas.
ocar.challenge: Brain-wide dynamics need an architectural map; zebrafish lacked an interactive atlas that combined many single-neuron reconstructions with co-registered transgene patterns and areal wiring.
ocar.action: In Neuron in 2019, Kunst, Laurell, Mokayes, Kramer, and Baier reconstructed over 2,000 individually GFP-labeled neurons, clustered morphologies, co-registered over 100 transgene patterns, annotated 72 non-overlapping brain regions, and derived an inter-areal wiring diagram, with virtual tract tracing in tectum and cerebellum.
ocar.resolution: The atlas yields a quantitative morphotype database with in vivo coordinates, an inter-areal wiring diagram as EM ground truth, and previously unknown tectal and cerebellar wiring principles from virtual tract tracing. It is presented as an evolving computational resource.
ocar.future_work: The authors call it essential for mapping function to structure in a vertebrate brain; expansion of neuron counts and transgenes is implied by ‘evolving’.

summaries.beginner: The team traced more than two thousand individual neurons in a baby zebrafish brain, grouped them by shape, and built a region-to-region wiring sketch. An interactive atlas lets others look up cells and predicted paths.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron in 2019, Kunst, Laurell, Mokayes, Kramer, and Baier published a 6 days-post-fertilization zebrafish cellular atlas from more than 2,000 GFP-labeled reconstructions. Neurons were clustered into morphotypes with in vivo coordinates, more than 100 transgene patterns were co-registered, and 72 brain regions were annotated. The resulting inter-areal wiring diagram is offered as ground truth for electron microscopy, and virtual tract tracing revealed previously unknown tectal and cerebellar wiring principles.
summaries.advanced: Wiring is inter-areal from light-microscopy reconstructions, not synapse-resolved EM. ‘Over 2,000’ neurons and ‘over 100’ transgenes and 72 regions are the stated counts. Catalog datasets include Drosophila larva and zebrafish; the paper is zebrafish (fly tag is likely a stream artifact). Stages include proofreading, infrastructure, and graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: The team traced more than two thousand individual neurons in a baby zebrafish brain, grouped them by shape, and built a region-to-region wiring sketch. An interactive atlas lets others look up cells and predicted paths.

ocar.opportunity: All body-wall motor neurons of the Drosophila larva are identified, so a complete proprioceptor–premotor–motor connectome could explain how the same motor neurons produce distinct behaviors.
ocar.challenge: Roles of most motor neurons in locomotion were untested, most premotor neurons unidentified, and proprioceptor–PMN–MN connectivity incomplete, leaving open how forward versus backward crawling arise.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2019, Zarin, Mark, Cardona, Litwin-Kumar, and Doe report a comprehensive larval proprioceptor–PMN–MN connectome, describe muscle/MN phase activity in forward and backward locomotion, identify connectivity motifs, validate some experimentally, and build a recurrent network model from the premotor pool.
ocar.resolution: Motifs could generate observed muscle phase relationships; proprioceptor–PMN wiring offered an anatomical account of proprioception promoting locomotor velocity; a candidate escape circuit was identified. The recurrent model produced the observed motor sequence, showing the identified premotor pool can generate two distinct behaviors via behavior-specific rhythms.
ocar.future_work: The authors conclude that different locomotor behaviors can arise from a specific premotor group; further experiments would test remaining unvalidated motifs and the escape-circuit candidate.

summaries.beginner: A fruit-fly maggot uses the same motor cells to crawl forward or backward. Mapping every sensory, premotor, and motor contact, then simulating them, shows one premotor team can play two different muscle rhythms.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2019 bioRxiv preprint, Zarin, Doe, Cardona, and colleagues present a Drosophila larva proprioceptor–premotor–motor connectome with phase activity for forward and backward crawling. They describe PMN–MN motifs (with selected validation), proprioceptor wiring that can promote speed, and a candidate escape circuit. A recurrent model using the identified premotor pool generated both behaviors.
summaries.advanced: Model sufficiency is for the identified premotor pool producing two rhythms, not a proof that no other neurons contribute in vivo. ‘Selected experimental validation’ means not all motifs were tested. Dataset is DS03 Drosophila larva. Stage is graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: A fruit-fly maggot uses the same motor cells to crawl forward or backward. Mapping every sensory, premotor, and motor contact, then simulating them, shows one premotor team can play two different muscle rhythms.

ocar.opportunity: Tens of thousands of single-neuron fluorescence images in FlyCircuit v1.2 can be turned into a neuron-to-neuron Drosophila brain network for community and centrality analysis.
ocar.challenge: Without a comprehensive brain-wide neural-network map, systems-level Drosophila function is hard to study, and image-based networks are not the same as synapse-resolved connectomes.
ocar.action: In Neuroinformatics in 2019, Shih, Lin, Wang, and colleagues built a network from 28,573 single-neuron images, then ran modularity and centrality analyses, small-world and rich-club tests, and loop enumeration.
ocar.resolution: Eight communities were identified (right/left olfaction, olfactory core, auditory, motor, pre-motor, left/right vision), with different functions dominating different centrality types. The network was overall small-world except two olfaction communities and motor, and a rich club’s innermost members mostly innervated the central complex. Numerous loops shorter than seven neurons were found.
ocar.future_work: The authors interpret loops and community-specific centralities as hypotheses about fly information processing; synapse-level data would be needed to confirm those paths.

summaries.beginner: Using more than 28,000 pictures of single fly neurons, the authors built a whole-brain contact map and found eight neighborhoods, including smell, vision, and motor groups. A richly connected club sits in the central complex.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroinformatics in 2019, Shih et al. constructed a Drosophila neuron-to-neuron network from 28,573 FlyCircuit v1.2 images. Modularity yielded eight communities; centrality types differed by function. Overall small-worldness held except two olfactory communities and motor. Innermost rich-club neurons mostly innervated the central complex, and many loops shorter than seven neurons were detected.
summaries.advanced: This is a light-microscopy, image-overlap/innervation network, not EM synapses. 28,573 images is the stated source count. Loop length bound is ‘smaller than seven neurons.’ Catalog stages are infrastructure and graph analysis; organism is fly.

plain_language_summary: Using more than 28,000 pictures of single fly neurons, the authors built a whole-brain contact map and found eight neighborhoods, including smell, vision, and motor groups. A richly connected club sits in the central complex.

ocar.opportunity: Electron microscopy needs multiplexed genetic reporters that do not rely on chemical precipitation or antibodies, which limit precision, penetration, and ultrastructure.
ocar.challenge: Ferritin’s iron core is small and hard to tell from cellular textures, and most EM gene reporters are not easily multiplexed or fully genetic.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2019, Sigmund, Pettinger, Kube, Schneider, and colleagues introduce the Quasibacillus thermotolerans encapsulin (QtEnc) as an iron-biomineralizing nanocompartment, determine its cryo-EM structure, show native cargo ferroxidase activity in mammalian cells, and train a deep-learning model to tell QtEnc (~44 nm) from Myxococcus xanthus encapsulin (~32 nm).
ocar.resolution: Qt monomers form T=4 icosahedral nanospheres ~44 nm across with putative pores at five- and threefold axes. Native cargo auto-targets the inner surface and sequesters iron in mammalian cells. QtEnc can be robustly differentiated from non-intermixing Mx encapsulin, enabling automated multiplexed TEM gene-reporter imaging.
ocar.future_work: The two-size reporter pair is a multiplexed TEM toolkit; additional encapsulins or organisms would extend the palette.

summaries.beginner: The authors import bacterial protein shells that store iron so they show up in electron-microscope pictures of mammalian cells. Two shell sizes can be told apart by a computer, giving two genetic labels without extra chemicals.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2019 bioRxiv preprint, Sigmund, Westmeyer, Dietz, and colleagues establish Quasibacillus thermotolerans encapsulin as a fully genetic electron-microscopy reporter. Cryo-electron reconstructions show T=4 particles about 44 nm across whose ferroxidase cargo sequesters iron in mammalian cells. A deep-learning model distinguishes them from about 32 nm Myxococcus xanthus encapsulins, enabling multiplexed conventional TEM gene reporting.
summaries.advanced: Diameters ~44 nm and ~32 nm and T=4 symmetry are from cryo-EM reconstructions as stated. ‘Robustly differentiated’ has no accuracy number in the abstract. This is a reporter-methods paper (preparation/acquisition/infrastructure; TEM), not a connectome. Multiplexing is demonstrated as two classes in mammalian cells.

plain_language_summary: The authors import bacterial protein shells that store iron so they show up in electron-microscope pictures of mammalian cells. Two shell sizes can be told apart by a computer, giving two genetic labels without extra chemicals.

ocar.opportunity: Platynereis larvae are small and transparent, so whole-body cell-type and circuit maps can include neuron classes missing from C. elegans and Drosophila, such as ciliary photoreceptors and noradrenergic neurons.
ocar.challenge: Cell-type diversity in this annelid needed a synthesis across gene-expression atlases, single-cell RNA-seq, serial EM connectomics, and functional experiments.
ocar.action: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2019, Williams and Jékely review neuronal cell types in Platynereis dumerilii and the methods used to define them, including experimental circuit analyses.
ocar.resolution: The review catalogs identified types and notes biology absent from major invertebrate models: ciliary locomotion, noradrenergic neurons, and ciliary photoreceptor cells.
ocar.future_work: Platynereis is positioned as a laboratory model whose cell-type list will grow with further atlas and circuit work.

summaries.beginner: A marine worm larva is clear enough to list its brain cell types across the whole body. Some of those types, including cells that sense light with cilia, do not exist in the usual worm and fly lab animals.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2019, Williams and Jékely review neuronal cell types in the marine annelid Platynereis dumerilii. Types have been defined with gene-expression atlases, single-cell RNA-seq, whole-body electron-microscopy connectomics, and functional experiments. They emphasize biology absent from C. elegans and Drosophila, including ciliary locomotion, noradrenergic neurons, and ciliary photoreceptors.
summaries.advanced: This is a review. Datasets tagged include C. elegans and Platynereis; the focus is Platynereis. Method tag is electron microscopy among others used in the literature surveyed.

plain_language_summary: A marine worm larva is clear enough to list its brain cell types across the whole body. Some of those types, including cells that sense light with cilia, do not exist in the usual worm and fly lab animals.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans connectome can be treated as a modular multilayer network, so one can ask how electrical, chemical, and extrasynaptic (‘wireless’) layers shape synchronization and chimera-like states.
ocar.challenge: Designed two-layer networks were already known to support chimera-like states; it was unclear whether the real three-layer worm topology, including wireless coupling, does the same.
ocar.action: In Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics in 2019, Pournaki, Merfort, Ruiz, Kouvaris, Hövel, and Hizanidis used Multilayer-Louvain communities on synaptic plus extrasynaptic layers and simulated coupled Hindmarsh–Rose neurons, quantifying local and global coherence. They also redefined communities from dynamical correlations.
ocar.resolution: Stronger wireless coupling decreased average coherence locally and globally and did not favor chimera-like states. Correlation-based communities were dominated by two large groups, which promoted chimera-like states and allowed linking neuron dynamics to functions such as motor activity.
ocar.future_work: The contrast between anatomical and dynamical communities is a method point: biological interpretation of chimeras depends on how modules are defined.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring has chemical links, electrical pores, and slower extrasynaptic signals. In a model, turning up the extrasynaptic coupling made the cells fire less in sync, while grouping cells by how they actually fired made split ‘chimera’ patterns easier to see.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics in 2019, Pournaki et al. simulate Hindmarsh–Rose neurons on a three-layer C. elegans connectome (electrical, chemical, extrasynaptic). Wireless coupling reduced local and global synchrony and disfavored chimera-like states. Communities from dynamical correlations, dominated by two large modules, promoted chimeras and mapped onto functions such as motor activity.
summaries.advanced: Results are from Hindmarsh–Rose simulations, not calcium imaging. Chimera-like states depend on community definition (Louvain versus correlation). Dataset is DS01 C. elegans. Stage is graph analysis. No numeric coupling strengths appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring has chemical links, electrical pores, and slower extrasynaptic signals. In a model, turning up the extrasynaptic coupling made the cells fire less in sync, while grouping cells by how they actually fired made split ‘chimera’ patterns easier to see.

ocar.opportunity: Head-direction cells in the Drosophila central complex implement a ring attractor, and homologous circuits in other insects share topography but differ in connectivity, so comparative modeling can test which details matter.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether the fly circuit is a general blueprint for heading computation or whether ecological differences produced distinct dynamics.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv in 2019, Pisokas, Heinze, and Webb modeled precise connectivity patterns of fruit-fly and locust head-direction circuits and compared speed of heading updates versus noise tolerance.
ocar.resolution: The locust circuit can also operate as a ring attractor. Connectivity-parameter differences make the fruit-fly circuit respond faster to heading changes, while the locust circuit is more noise-tolerant. Subtle projection-pattern differences therefore change performance.
ocar.future_work: The authors emphasize the need for a comparative approach; additional species would test whether speed-versus-robustness trade-offs track ecology.

summaries.beginner: Flies and locusts both keep an internal compass in a similar brain region, but the wiring details differ. Models suggest the fly compass updates faster, while the locust compass shrugs off noise better.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2019 bioRxiv preprint, Pisokas, Heinze, and Webb compare ring-attractor models of Drosophila and locust central-complex heading circuits using species-specific connectivity. Both can function as ring attractors. Parameter differences yield faster heading responses in the fly circuit and greater noise tolerance in the locust circuit, showing that small projection changes affect performance.
summaries.advanced: This is computational comparison constrained by published connectivity, not new EM. ‘Faster’ and ‘more tolerant’ are relative model outcomes without numeric latencies in the abstract. Organism tag is fly; locust is the comparison species. Stage is graph analysis.

plain_language_summary: Flies and locusts both keep an internal compass in a similar brain region, but the wiring details differ. Models suggest the fly compass updates faster, while the locust compass shrugs off noise better.

ocar.opportunity: New reconstructions produce connectomes large enough that interactive, publication-grade, and downstream-simulation analyses are all required to make them usable.
ocar.challenge: Unlike genomics, connectomics lacks standard analyses and file formats; groups use Matlab, R, Python, or C++ with idiosyncratic readers, and long-term archival is unfunded. Downstream simulators cannot swallow raw reconstruction detail.
ocar.action: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits in 2018, Scheffer reviews three analysis categories—interactive reconstruction tools, reproducible publication analyses, and import into simulation or machine learning—and discusses intelligent reduction of detail and merging with genetic or optical data.
ocar.resolution: In the short term, the practical path is to publish analysis code and data interfaces. In the long term, a central connectome facility analogous to NCBI is proposed. Two import problems are highlighted: reducing huge detail and merging non-EM measurements.
ocar.future_work: Scheffer’s agenda is standards, archives, and reduction/merge tooling as connectomics becomes more common.

summaries.beginner: Huge wiring maps are useless without software to explore them, to document how figures were made, and to simplify them for simulations. This article surveys those needs and argues for shared archives, the way genomes already have.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits in 2018, Scheffer reviews analysis tools for large connectomes: interactive reconstruction aids, reproducible publication workflows, and export to simulation or ML. He notes the lack of standard formats versus genomics, recommends publishing code plus data interfaces, and proposes a future central archive. Import requires intelligent detail reduction and merging with non-EM data.
summaries.advanced: This is a tools/opinion survey, not a methods benchmark. No specific dataset performance is reported. Stages are infrastructure and modeling.

plain_language_summary: Huge wiring maps are useless without software to explore them, to document how figures were made, and to simplify them for simulations. This article surveys those needs and argues for shared archives, the way genomes already have.

ocar.opportunity: Network control theory offers a quantitative way to relate C. elegans structure to how the nervous system steers behavior, following a 2017 Nature application of the framework.
ocar.challenge: The math, computations, and experiments of network control are unfamiliar to many worm biologists, and the framework’s capabilities and limits need a plain FAQ.
ocar.action: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2018, Towlson, Vértes, Yan, Chew, Walker, Schafer, and Barabási review network control as applied to C. elegans, covering theory, computation, and experiment, and provide Python code for organism-specific exploration.
ocar.resolution: The FAQ presents control as a predictive structure–function framework that can unite diverse worm datasets, while stating current limitations and likely improvements. It is part of a ‘connectome to behaviour’ discussion meeting issue.
ocar.future_work: The authors discuss next advances and improvements of the control framework and invite exploration via the released code.

summaries.beginner: This explainer asks how a worm’s wiring diagram determines which cells one would need to nudge to steer the animal. It translates a math framework called network control into practical answers and sharing code.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2018, Towlson, Vértes, Yan, Barabási, Schafer, and colleagues provide an FAQ on network control applied to C. elegans, building on Yan et al. 2017 in Nature. They review theoretical, computational, and experimental aspects, current limits, and likely advances. Python code is released so readers can explore control principles in this organism. The article is part of a discussion-meeting issue on modelling C. elegans from connectome to behaviour.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/FAQ of a framework, not a new connectome. Predictive claims inherit the assumptions of linear network control as used in the 2017 paper. Dataset tag is DS01 C. elegans. Stage is infrastructure.

plain_language_summary: This explainer asks how a worm’s wiring diagram determines which cells one would need to nudge to steer the animal. It translates a math framework called network control into practical answers and sharing code.

ocar.opportunity: The zebrafish lateral-line neuromast has a restricted, consistent innervation pattern, so complete hair-cell-to-nerve connectomes can be compared across individuals, stages, and genotypes.
ocar.challenge: How directional hair cells wire to afferent terminals, and how mutants scramble that logic, needed synapse-resolution maps from multiple specimens.
ocar.action: In eLife in 2018 (catalog journal field lists bioRxiv), Dow, Jacobo, Hossain, Siletti, and Hudspeth used serial block-face SEM to reconstruct neuromast connectomes from multiple fish, then examined vangl2 mutants and Notch-overexpressing larvae.
ocar.resolution: Each nerve terminal received input from hair cells of a single directional sensitivity; innervation was redundant; terminals showed a dominance hierarchy. vangl2 mutation randomized sibling hair-cell position and orientation but wiring specificity remained. Notch overexpression yielded uniformly oriented, uniformly innervating siblings, implicating Notch in wiring specificity.
ocar.future_work: The neuromast is offered as a microcircuit template; further genotypes would test which polarity versus identity cues Notch and Vangl2 separate.

summaries.beginner: In a simple fish touch organ, each nerve ending listens to hair cells that prefer one direction, with backup copies and a pecking order. Breaking a polarity gene scrambled cell positions but not that matching rule; pushing Notch made matching too uniform.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife in 2018, Dow, Jacobo, Hossain, Siletti, and Hudspeth reconstruct zebrafish lateral-line neuromast connectomes with serial block-face scanning electron microscopy from multiple specimens. Afferent terminals are direction-specific, redundant, and hierarchically dominant. vangl2 mutants have randomly placed, randomly oriented sibling hair cells that still wire specifically, whereas Notch overexpression produces uniformly oriented, uniformly innervating siblings, implicating Notch in wiring specificity.
summaries.advanced: Conclusions combine wild-type maps with two genetic manipulations. ‘Hierarchy of dominance’ is not quantified in the abstract. Catalog journal lists bioRxiv; DOI is eLife. Dataset DS15 zebrafish; methods SEM; stages sectioning and acquisition.

plain_language_summary: In a simple fish touch organ, each nerve ending listens to hair cells that prefer one direction, with backup copies and a pecking order. Breaking a polarity gene scrambled cell positions but not that matching rule; pushing Notch made matching too uniform.

ocar.opportunity: Neuron reconstructions and macroscale tract data now exist for human, mouse, and rat, so one can test whether microscale cellular complexity tracks how many long-range projections an area sends.
ocar.challenge: Microscale axons/dendrites/synapses and macroscale interareal projections are rarely studied together, even though both shape function.
ocar.action: In Brain Connectivity in 2018, Scholtens, Barrett, and van den Heuvel combined NeuroMorpho.org reconstructions with tract-tracing (rat, mouse) and in vivo diffusion MRI (human) connectomes, correlating neuronal complexity with white-matter projection numbers.
ocar.resolution: Across human, mouse, and rat, cortical variation in neuronal complexity explained significant proportions of variation in the number of white-matter projections. The authors see a conserved micro–macro connectivity relationship as central to mammalian architecture, consistent with earlier cat, macaque, and human reports that larger, more complex pyramids have more corticocortical connections.
ocar.future_work: The cross-scale association is correlative; causal tests would need developmental or comparative perturbations of neuronal morphology.

summaries.beginner: Brain areas whose cells have more elaborate branches also tend to send more long-distance cables. The authors find that pattern in human scans and in mouse and rat tracing maps.
summaries.intermediate: In Brain Connectivity in 2018, Scholtens, Barrett, and van den Heuvel relate NeuroMorpho neuron reconstructions to macroscale connectivity from rodent tract-tracing and human diffusion MRI. Across human, mouse, and rat, neuronal complexity accounted for significant cortical variation in white-matter projection counts. The result extends earlier reports in cat, macaque, and human that larger, more complex pyramids have more corticocortical connections.
summaries.advanced: ‘Significant proportions’ is not given as R² in the abstract. Human macroscale data are diffusion MRI, not tracers; rodents are tract-tracing. Catalog organism is mouse; the paper is three-species. Stages are proofreading and infrastructure.

plain_language_summary: Brain areas whose cells have more elaborate branches also tend to send more long-distance cables. The authors find that pattern in human scans and in mouse and rat tracing maps.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroscience applications need shared middleware to visualize models and data and to run simulations in the browser or on the desktop, from C. elegans to fly anatomy to NEURON networks.
ocar.challenge: Each community built separate UIs for OSB, Virtual Fly Brain, NEURON, and NetPyNE, duplicating infrastructure for data sources, repositories, and simulators.
ocar.action: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2018, Cantarelli, Marin, Quintana, Earnshaw, Court, Gleeson, Dura-Bernal, Silver, and Idili present Geppetto, with domain-agnostic model/data abstractions, a backend for external sources and simulators, and a customizable frontend, underpinning OSB, VFB, NEURON-UI, and NetPyNE-UI.
ocar.resolution: Geppetto is described as reusable modular open platform covering visualization and simulation control in a highly accessible way, including NeuroML models on OSB and Drosophila anatomy/imaging on VFB.
ocar.future_work: As part of a C. elegans cellular-resolution modelling issue, the platform is meant to keep expanding the set of connected simulators and data sources.

summaries.beginner: Geppetto is shared software that many brain websites sit on, so you can view worm or fly data and run models in a browser. Each project does not have to reinvent the same controls.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2018, Cantarelli, Marin, Quintana, Gleeson, Silver, Idili, and colleagues introduce Geppetto, middleware for visualizing neuroscience models and data and for managing simulations. It underpins Open Source Brain, Virtual Fly Brain, NEURON-UI, and NetPyNE-UI through shared abstractions. A backend connects to external data sources, model repositories, and simulators, with a customizable frontend. The article is part of a C. elegans cellular-resolution modelling issue.
summaries.advanced: This is infrastructure, not a biological result. Dataset tag is DS01 C. elegans among users of the platform. Stages include segmentation, infrastructure, graph analysis, and modeling—reflecting the apps it hosts rather than a single pipeline experiment.

plain_language_summary: Geppetto is shared software that many brain websites sit on, so you can view worm or fly data and run models in a browser. Each project does not have to reinvent the same controls.

ocar.opportunity: Network neuroscience usually studies pairwise links, but cavities and higher-order structure in connectomes, synapses, and genomic contacts may be crucial for function and are visible to persistent homology.
ocar.challenge: Pairwise graph tools cannot encode interacting sets of nodes (simplices) or the cavities those relations create, so network neuroscientists need an accessible introduction to applied topology.
ocar.action: In Network Neuroscience in 2018, Sizemore, Phillips-Cremins, Ghrist, and Bassett explain persistent homology, then demonstrate calculations on the mouse structural connectome, C. elegans synapses, and genomic interaction data, and point to newer mathematics ready for neural systems.
ocar.resolution: The paper is a pedagogical and demonstrative introduction: it shows how a filtration of a weighted network yields a global descriptor of evolving cavities, with worked neural and genomic examples.
ocar.future_work: The authors highlight avenues for future work and new topological methods they consider ready for neuroscience applications.

summaries.beginner: Ordinary network pictures only show pairs of connected points. This tutorial explains a branch of math that also finds holes and groups of several points acting together, with examples from mouse brain wiring, worm contacts, and DNA folding.
summaries.intermediate: In Network Neuroscience in 2018, Sizemore, Phillips-Cremins, Ghrist, and Bassett introduce persistent homology for network neuroscientists. Data are encoded as simplicial complexes, and evolving cavities are tracked through a filtration such as a weighted connectome. Worked examples use the mouse structural connectome, C. elegans synapses, and chromatin interaction data, with pointers to newer topological methods.
summaries.advanced: This is an exposition with demonstrative calculations, not a new biological discovery paper. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans among the examples; mouse connectome and genomic data are also used. Stage is graph analysis. No numeric Betti numbers appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Ordinary network pictures only show pairs of connected points. This tutorial explains a branch of math that also finds holes and groups of several points acting together, with examples from mouse brain wiring, worm contacts, and DNA folding.

ocar.opportunity: Realistic models need wiring diagrams at cellular resolution with quantified accuracy, i.e., connectomics of identified pre- and postsynaptic neurons and their synapses.
ocar.challenge: Submicron caliber, 3D complexity, packing density, and long-range axons make complete maps technically demanding and require multi-scale labeling and imaging with increasing throughput.
ocar.action: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy in 2016, Kisvárday, Lyon, Rockland, Cazemier, Clascá, and Tiesinga review then-new high-resolution tools: molecular labels (including synapse-specific ones), brain clearing, and novel microscopy, and they assess each against the qualities needed to decode circuit organization.
ocar.resolution: The review inventories tools for mapping somata, dendrites, axons, synapses, and gap junctions, rates their strengths, and notes outstanding issues such as structure–function relations and model complexity.
ocar.future_work: The authors close with a brief outlook for neuroanatomy, computational methods, and network modeling, including structure–function and the complexity of neural models.

summaries.beginner: To draw a brain’s true wiring, scientists must see whole cells and their tiny contacts, which is technically brutal. This review surveys new dyes, clearing recipes, and microscopes meant to make that job possible.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy in 2016, Kisvárday, Lyon, Rockland, Cazemier, Clascá, and Tiesinga review connectomic methods at cellular resolution. They cover molecular labels (including synapse-specific reagents), brain clearing, and then-new microscopy. Tools are assessed against the need to measure soma, dendrites, axons, synapses, and gap junctions at increasing throughput, with notes on structure–function and model complexity.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods review from 2016; many listed tools have since evolved. No new dataset is presented. Axis is biological application / connectomics. Organism and dataset tags are empty.

plain_language_summary: To draw a brain’s true wiring, scientists must see whole cells and their tiny contacts, which is technically brutal. This review surveys new dyes, clearing recipes, and microscopes meant to make that job possible.

ocar.opportunity: Three-dimensional electron microscopy had made imaging ever-larger tissue blocks realistic, bringing complete mapping of neuronal circuits in parts of brains within reach.
ocar.challenge: Analysis of those volumes, not acquisition, was already limiting the neuroscience one could extract from cellular connectomics.
ocar.action: In e-Neuroforum in 2016, Helmstaedter briefly surveys the state of cellular-precision connectomics: what imaging breakthroughs enabled, what had been learned, and what remained in reach.
ocar.resolution: The overview summarizes then-current knowledge, emphasizing that analysis—not imaging—was the bottleneck for insight from large 3D EM datasets.
ocar.future_work: The piece asks which insights are in reach once analysis catches up to acquisition.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can now photograph ever-larger chunks of brain. This short overview says the hard part is no longer taking the pictures but making sense of them.
summaries.intermediate: In e-Neuroforum in 2016, Helmstaedter reviews cellular-precision connectomics after three-dimensional electron microscopy made large-block imaging realistic. He argues that data analysis, not acquisition, already limited the neuroscience extractable from those volumes. The overview summarizes what the field had learned and which insights remained in reach.
summaries.advanced: This is a brief 2016 overview, not a primary reconstruction. Method tag is electron microscopy. No volumes or error rates are cited in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can now photograph ever-larger chunks of brain. This short overview says the hard part is no longer taking the pictures but making sense of them.

ocar.opportunity: Skeleton tracing of neuronal fibers across serial EM sections is a core proofreading task that could be faster if the tracer’s gaze itself defined the path.
ocar.challenge: Linking tubular objects through consecutive ultrathin sections is slow with conventional annotation; high-speed 3D browsing needs an intuitive way to stay locked on one fiber.
ocar.action: At CHI in 2016, Templier, Bektas, and Hahnloser present Eye-Trace: users ‘fly’ through volumetric EM with a gamepad while a desktop eyetracker records continuous foveation on a fiber, converting gaze into 3D skeleton coordinates.
ocar.resolution: In a participant experiment, tracing accuracy was about the radius of the traced fibers at browsing speeds up to 40 brain sections per second.
ocar.future_work: The method is a human-computer tracing interface; integrating it with automated segmentation would be the natural production path.

summaries.beginner: Instead of clicking along a neuron in a 3D electron-microscope stack, a person looks at the fiber while steering with a gamepad. An eye tracker turns that gaze into a traced path, at up to 40 sections per second, with errors about as big as the fiber’s width.
summaries.intermediate: At the 2016 CHI conference, Templier, Bektas, and Hahnloser introduced Eye-Trace for volumetric EM annotation. Gaze while flying through serial brain sections is recorded and converted to 3D skeletons. A user study reported accuracy on the order of fiber radius at up to 40 sections per second.
summaries.advanced: Accuracy ‘about the respective radiuses’ is the stated result; no pixel error table is in the abstract. Speeds up to 40 sections/s are browsing/tracing speeds in the experiment, not automated segmentation throughput. Stages are segmentation and proofreading; method is electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: Instead of clicking along a neuron in a 3D electron-microscope stack, a person looks at the fiber while steering with a gamepad. An eye tracker turns that gaze into a traced path, at up to 40 sections per second, with errors about as big as the fiber’s width.

ocar.opportunity: Light- and electron-microscopy modalities had begun contributing essential connectome data across organisms, but only because acquisition and analysis of large datasets had also advanced.
ocar.challenge: Connectomic datasets already showed unimaginable synaptic complexity at EM scale and complicated uni- and reciprocal networks at meso/macro scales, demanding better handling and automation.
ocar.action: In Microscopy in 2016, Ohno, Katoh, Saitoh, and Saitoh review recent imaging and analysis innovations for connectomics and the picture they had produced of brain circuitry.
ocar.resolution: They describe unidirectional and reciprocal cerebral networks at macroscopic and mesoscopic levels and extreme synaptic complexity at EM level, while stressing the need for efficient handling and automated analysis. Multidisciplinary combinations of imaging modalities are proposed to ask whether complete connectomes can explain basic and higher human brain functions.
ocar.future_work: The review flags substantial remaining methodology needs and the open question of whether a complete connectome elucidates human brain function.
